concepts.label: Artificial Intelligence
concepts.summary: Systems that perform tasks we associate with human intelligence — perceiving, predicting, reasoning, and acting.
concepts.explanation: This is the root of the map. 'AI' is not one technique but a family of them, and the branches below trace how the field actually stacks up. Foundations asks what kind of intelligence a task needs. Neural Networks and Transformers explain how today's dominant models learn and run. Retrieval, Customization, and Agents are about making a general model useful on your problem. Security, Practice, and Governance are about deploying it responsibly. Expand any branch to move from the basics toward the engineering, and follow the dashed relationship edges to see how ideas in different branches connect.
keyPoints: AI is an umbrella: rule systems, classical ML, deep neural networks, and generative/agentic LLMs are all 'AI' with very different mechanics.
The dominant paradigm today is the neural network — functions with millions to trillions of tunable weights learned from data.
The left-to-right depth of this map mirrors learning order: understand the model first, then how to feed, extend, and govern it.

The branches are laid out for learning order, not strict containment: neural networks are a kind of machine learning and Transformers are a kind of neural network, but each gets its own branch so you can go deep without descending through everything above it. The dashed relationship edges restore those 'is a kind of' connections.
Nodes marked ✎ were written for this guide to fill gaps the 36 lessons don't cover directly.

concepts.label: Kinds of Intelligence
concepts.summary: Four ways to make a decision at scale — humans, rules, classical ML, and generative AI — arranged on a spectrum of determinism, not a ladder.
concepts.explanation: Before reaching for AI, it helps to see that automation has four distinct modes, each with a different trade-off. A human brings judgement, handles ambiguity, and can be held accountable, but does not scale. Hard-coded rules are exact, fast, and fully auditable, but brittle when reality doesn't match the rules. Classical machine learning finds statistical patterns in structured data, useful when the logic is too complex to write by hand. Generative AI handles unstructured input and produces flexible output, but is non-deterministic and hard to explain. The mistake is treating these as a ladder where the newest option is always best; they are options, and the right one depends on the task. The deciding question is how much non-determinism the use case can tolerate.
keyPoints: Humans handle judgement, ambiguity and accountability; rules give exact, auditable, deterministic logic; ML finds patterns in structured data; generative AI handles unstructured input with flexible output.
The real design question is 'how much non-determinism can you tolerate?' — a fraud rule that must be explainable in court is a bad fit for a probabilistic model.
Most robust systems are hybrids: rules for the parts that must be exact, ML or LLMs for the parts that are fuzzy.
Every non-deterministic component adds cost you keep paying: monitoring for drift, a golden evaluation set, and a fallback when it is wrong.

concepts.label: Machine Learning
concepts.summary: Instead of writing rules by hand, you show a model examples and let it fit a function that maps inputs to outputs.
concepts.explanation: Machine learning flips the usual logic of programming. Rather than a human writing the rules, you provide examples and an algorithm searches for a function that reproduces them and generalises to new cases. It comes in three main flavours: supervised learning trains on labelled input-output pairs; unsupervised learning finds hidden structure in unlabelled data (clustering, dimensionality reduction); reinforcement learning learns from reward signals earned by acting in an environment. A model has parameters, which are learned from data, and hyperparameters, which you set; training adjusts the parameters to minimise a loss that measures error. The central challenge is generalisation — a model that merely memorises the training set (overfitting) will fail on new data, which is why you always evaluate on a held-out test set. Classical ML methods like gradient-boosted trees still beat neural networks on tabular data; deep learning took over for perception and language.
keyPoints: Supervised learning trains on labelled pairs (input → correct output); unsupervised learning finds structure with no labels; reinforcement learning learns from reward signals.
A model has parameters (learned from data) and hyperparameters (set by you). Training minimises a loss function that measures how wrong the predictions are.
The core risk is generalisation: a model that memorises the training set (overfits) fails on new data. You hold out a test set to measure real performance.
Classical ML (linear/logistic regression, decision trees, gradient boosting, SVMs) still wins on tabular data; neural networks dominate perception and language.

concepts.label: Reinforcement Learning (RLHF & RLVR)
concepts.summary: Learning from consequences rather than labelled answers — the paradigm that now shapes an LLM's behaviour and, increasingly, its reasoning.
concepts.explanation: Reinforcement learning is the third paradigm of machine learning, and it has become the decisive one for frontier models. Instead of learning from labelled input-output pairs, an agent takes actions in an environment, receives a reward signal, and adjusts its policy to earn more reward over time — learning from consequences rather than from a teacher's answer key. Classic RL powered game-playing systems like AlphaGo; for language models it now appears in two forms that matter enormously. RLHF (reinforcement learning from human feedback) trains a reward model on human preference comparisons and then optimises the LLM against it, which is what actually instils helpfulness, tone, and refusal behaviour — the step that turned a raw pretrained model into a usable assistant. RLVR (RL from verifiable rewards) goes further and is the engine behind modern reasoning models: instead of a learned reward model, the reward comes from automatically checkable outcomes — did the maths come out right, did the code pass its tests — which lets the model be trained to reason through problems without anyone hand-labelling the reasoning steps. This is why post-training is now treated as a pillar of model development alongside pretraining, not an afterthought.
keyPoints: RL learns from a reward signal earned by acting, not from labelled answers: the model tries something, sees the consequence, and updates its policy.
RLHF trains a reward model on human preference comparisons, then optimises the LLM against it — this is what produces helpfulness, tone and refusals.
RLVR (verifiable rewards) uses automatically checkable outcomes — maths that checks out, code that passes tests — and is how modern reasoning models are trained to think.
Because reasoning ability can be trained this way, post-training is now a pillar of frontier model development alongside pretraining, not a finishing touch.

concepts.label: Neurosymbolic AI
concepts.summary: Combining neural pattern recognition with symbolic logic: neural perception feeds a reasoning engine that follows explicit rules.
concepts.explanation: Neural networks and symbolic AI have opposite strengths and weaknesses. A neural network learns statistical patterns from data — it is robust to messy input but opaque, and it recognises patterns without genuinely 'understanding' or reasoning about them. Symbolic AI encodes knowledge as explicit rules and logic — it is transparent and exact, but it shatters on exceptions the rules never anticipated. Neurosymbolic AI stitches the two together: the neural part turns raw, unstructured input into clean symbols, and a symbolic reasoning engine then applies logic to those symbols. This gives a system both the flexibility of learning and the explainability of rules. Meta-learning takes it further, letting the symbolic layer revise its own rules through reasoning rather than requiring the whole network to be retrained.
keyPoints: Symbolic AI encodes knowledge as explicit rules and logic — transparent and exact, but brittle when reality does not match the rules.
Neural networks learn statistical patterns from data — robust to messy input, but opaque and prone to confident mistakes.
The hybrid uses the network to turn raw input into symbols, then a logic engine reasons over them, giving both flexibility and explainability.
Meta-learning lets the symbolic layer update its own rules through reasoning, rather than needing everything retrained.

concepts.label: The Neuron
concepts.summary: The atom of a neural network: it weights its inputs, sums them with a bias, and passes the result through an activation function.
concepts.explanation: A neuron is a small mathematical function, and every neural network is built entirely from copies of it. It receives a vector of input numbers, multiplies each by a learned weight, adds them together with a learned bias, and pushes that sum through an activation function to produce a single output number — compactly, output = activation(w·x + b). The weights are where learning lives: a large weight means that input strongly influences the neuron's output, so the pattern of weights encodes what the neuron has learned to care about. Before any of this can happen, real-world data (an image, a word, a row of a spreadsheet) must be converted into a numeric vector the neuron can multiply. The bias shifts the threshold at which the neuron activates, and the activation function decides how the raw weighted sum is squashed into an output.
keyPoints: A neuron is just a function: output = activation(w·x + b), where w are weights, x is the input vector, and b is the bias.
Weights encode learned importance — a large weight means that input strongly moves the neuron's output.
Real-world data must first be turned into a vector of numbers (a feature vector) before a neuron can process it.
The bias shifts the threshold at which the neuron 'fires'; the activation function decides how the weighted sum is squashed into an output.

concepts.label: Layers & Nonlinearity
concepts.summary: Stacking layers of neurons lets a network compose simple features into complex ones — but only because activations are nonlinear.
concepts.explanation: A single neuron can only draw a straight-line boundary, which is far too simple for real problems. Networks get their power by organising neurons into layers — an input layer, one or more hidden layers, and an output layer — where each layer's outputs feed the next. Within a layer, different neurons specialise on different features; across layers, the network composes those features into progressively more abstract concepts (edges, then shapes, then objects). The crucial ingredient is nonlinearity: if the activation function were linear, stacking layers would mathematically collapse into a single linear function and depth would buy nothing. Nonlinear activations like ReLU or sigmoid let each layer bend the representation, which is what allows a deep network to approximate extremely complex relationships.
keyPoints: Without a nonlinear activation, stacking layers collapses to a single linear function — depth would add nothing.
Nonlinear activations (sigmoid, ReLU) let each layer bend the representation, so deep networks can approximate very complex functions.
Neurons in one layer learn to detect different patterns; later layers combine those into higher-level concepts.
A network is organised as an input layer, one or more hidden layers, and an output layer.

concepts.label: Backpropagation & Gradient Descent
concepts.summary: How a network learns: measure the error, compute each weight's contribution to it, and nudge every weight to reduce it.
concepts.explanation: Training a network means finding weights that make its outputs match the desired ones, and this is done by a two-part loop. First, a loss function measures how wrong the current output is — cross-entropy is the standard choice for classification and next-token prediction because it punishes confident wrong answers heavily. Second, gradient descent adjusts the weights: it computes the gradient of the loss with respect to each weight (the direction that would increase error) and steps each weight the opposite way, scaled by a learning rate. Backpropagation is the efficient algorithm that computes all those gradients at once by applying the chain rule from calculus, propagating the error backwards from the output through every layer so each weight gets its exact share of the blame. This loop runs over mini-batches of data for many epochs, and it is the same procedure that trains everything from a single neuron to a trillion-parameter language model.
keyPoints: Gradient descent: compute the gradient of the loss with respect to each weight, then step each weight a little way downhill (scaled by the learning rate).
Backpropagation applies the chain rule from calculus to propagate the error backwards through the layers, giving every weight its share of the blame efficiently.
Cross-entropy loss is the standard for classification and next-token prediction; it punishes confident wrong answers heavily.
Training runs in mini-batches over many epochs; too high a learning rate diverges, too low is slow. This same loop trains everything from one neuron to a trillion-parameter LLM.

concepts.label: CNNs & RNNs
concepts.summary: The two architectures that dominated deep learning before Transformers: CNNs for spatial data, RNNs for sequences.
concepts.explanation: Before the Transformer, two specialised architectures carried deep learning. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) exploit spatial structure: they slide small learned filters across an image and share those weights across every position, so a feature like an edge is detected wherever it appears. Stacking convolutions builds up from edges to textures to whole objects, which made CNNs the backbone of computer vision. Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) handle sequences — text, audio, time series — by carrying a hidden state from one time step to the next, letting earlier inputs influence later ones. Their weakness is that they process a sequence strictly in order and struggle to connect distant elements (the vanishing-gradient problem); LSTMs and GRUs eased this but the sequential bottleneck capped their speed and scale. The Transformer replaced recurrence with attention, processing an entire sequence in parallel, which is exactly why it scaled where RNNs plateaued.
keyPoints: Convolutional neural networks slide small learned filters across an image, sharing weights to detect edges, textures and shapes regardless of position.
Recurrent neural networks carry a hidden state from one time step to the next, letting them model sequences — but they process tokens strictly in order.
RNNs struggle with long-range dependencies (the vanishing-gradient problem); LSTMs and GRUs helped, but sequential processing still capped their speed.
The Transformer replaced recurrence with attention, processing a whole sequence in parallel — which is why it scaled where RNNs stalled.

concepts.label: Graph Neural Networks
concepts.summary: Networks that learn from connected data — nodes joined by edges — by passing messages between neighbours.
concepts.explanation: Much real-world data is neither a grid (like an image) nor a sequence (like text) but a graph: social networks, molecules, knowledge bases, road maps. A graph is a set of nodes joined by edges, typically encoded as an adjacency matrix. Graph neural networks learn a vector embedding for each node that captures both the node's own features and the structure of its neighbourhood. The core operation is message passing: each node gathers ('aggregates') information from its neighbours and updates its own representation, and repeating this over several layers lets information travel further across the graph. The main architectures differ in how they aggregate — GCN averages neighbour features, GraphSAGE samples a fixed number of neighbours to scale to huge graphs, GAT weights neighbours using attention, and GIN sums them, which is provably the most expressive at telling graph structures apart. Graph Transformers apply attention across the whole graph, using the same query/key/value machinery found in language models.
keyPoints: A graph is nodes + edges, encoded as an adjacency matrix; GNNs learn an embedding for each node that reflects both its features and its neighbourhood.
Message passing is the core operation: each node aggregates information from neighbours, then updates itself — repeated for several layers to reach further out.
Architectures differ by how they aggregate: GCN averages, GraphSAGE samples neighbours to scale, GAT weights neighbours with attention, GIN sums (the most expressive).
Graph Transformers apply attention across the whole graph, and the query/key/value machinery is the same idea used in language Transformers.

concepts.label: Transformer Architecture
concepts.summary: The architecture behind essentially every modern LLM: it drops recurrence and processes a whole sequence at once via self-attention.
concepts.explanation: The Transformer is the design that made modern language models possible. Its key move is abandoning the step-by-step recurrence of RNNs: instead of reading a sequence one token at a time, it takes the whole sequence at once and uses self-attention to let every token look at every other token directly. Input tokens are turned into embeddings, combined with positional information (so order isn't lost), and passed through a stack of identical layers, each containing a self-attention block and a feed-forward block. Because attention is computed in parallel across the sequence, Transformers train dramatically faster on GPUs than sequential RNNs — the practical reason they could be scaled to billions of parameters. The 'decoder-only' variant used by the GPT family adds causal masking so each token can only attend to earlier tokens, which is precisely what enables left-to-right text generation. Depth, width, and enormous training data are what turn this architecture into a capable model.
keyPoints: Input tokens become embeddings plus positional information, then flow through a stack of identical layers, each with a self-attention block and a feed-forward block.
Because attention sees the whole sequence in parallel, Transformers train far faster on modern GPUs than sequential RNNs — the key to scaling to billions of parameters.
'Decoder-only' models (the GPT family) use causal (masked) attention so each token attends only to earlier tokens, which is what makes next-token generation possible.
Depth (many layers) plus width (large hidden size) plus scale of data is what turns this architecture into a capable language model.

concepts.label: Attention (Q·K·V)
concepts.summary: The mechanism that lets each token decide which other tokens matter to it, using queries, keys, and values.
concepts.explanation: Attention is the engine of the Transformer, and the idea is intuitive once broken down. Every token produces three vectors: a query (what am I looking for?), a key (what do I offer?), and a value (what content do I carry?). To build a token's new, context-aware representation, its query is compared against the keys of all tokens to produce a set of scores; those scores are normalised with a softmax into weights that sum to one; and the token's output becomes a weighted blend of everyone's values. High weight means 'this other token is relevant to me', which is how a model resolves what 'it' refers to, or links a question to the answer that appeared earlier in the text. Multi-head attention runs several of these operations in parallel, each free to learn a different kind of relationship, then concatenates the results. The one catch is cost: comparing every token to every other makes attention scale with the square of sequence length, which is exactly why long context is expensive and why optimisations like the KV cache exist.
keyPoints: For each token: score its query against all keys, softmax the scores into weights that sum to 1, then take a weighted sum of the values.
This is how a model resolves 'it' to the right noun or links a question to its answer earlier in the text — relevant tokens get high weight.
Multi-head attention runs several attention operations in parallel, each learning a different kind of relationship, then concatenates them.
Attention cost grows with the square of sequence length, which is why long context is expensive and why the KV cache and PagedAttention exist.

concepts.label: Tokens & Next-Token Prediction
concepts.summary: An LLM splits text into tokens and repeatedly predicts the most likely next one; fluent output is that loop run thousands of times.
concepts.explanation: An LLM never sees words the way we do, and it does not 'understand' in the human sense. Text is first broken into tokens — sub-word fragments — and the model's entire job is to output a probability distribution over its vocabulary for the next token given everything so far. Generation is autoregressive: sample one token, append it, feed the longer sequence back in, and predict again, repeating until the response is complete. Because the objective is simply 'what token likely comes next', the model is fundamentally syntactic — it captures the statistical form of language, not grounded truth — which is the deep reason it can produce fluent, confident, and wrong output. A sampling parameter called temperature controls how much randomness is allowed: low temperature makes the model focused and repetitive, high temperature makes it more creative and more error-prone.
keyPoints: Text is tokenised into sub-word units; the model outputs a probability distribution over its whole vocabulary for the next token.
Generation is autoregressive: sample one token, append it, feed the longer sequence back in, predict again.
Because it predicts statistically likely continuations, an LLM is syntactic — it models the form of language, not grounded meaning, which is the root of hallucination.
Temperature controls randomness in sampling: low is focused and repetitive, high is creative and riskier.

concepts.label: LLM Training Pipeline
concepts.summary: How a raw Transformer becomes a helpful assistant: pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, then alignment from feedback.
concepts.explanation: A freshly initialised Transformer knows nothing; turning it into a useful assistant happens in three stages. Pretraining runs next-token prediction over trillions of tokens of text, and in the process the model absorbs grammar, facts, and reasoning patterns — this stage consumes almost all of the compute and happens once. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) then continues training on a smaller, curated set of instruction-and-ideal-response pairs, teaching the model to follow instructions rather than merely autocomplete. Finally, alignment (RLHF, or its AI-feedback variant RLAIF) trains a reward model on human preferences and optimises the LLM to produce answers people rate more highly; this is what shapes its tone, helpfulness, safety, and refusal behaviour. A crucial consequence of all this is that the model's knowledge is frozen at its training cutoff — anything newer, or anything private to you, has to arrive through retrieval or context at run time, not through the weights.
keyPoints: Pretraining: next-token prediction over trillions of tokens teaches grammar, facts and reasoning patterns — this is where almost all the compute goes, once.
Supervised fine-tuning (SFT): continue training on curated (instruction, ideal response) pairs so the model follows instructions instead of just autocompleting.
Alignment (RLHF / RLAIF): train a reward model on preferences, then optimise the LLM to produce responses humans (or another AI) rate higher — this shapes tone, safety and refusals.
Everything after pretraining is called post-training, and it is now a pillar in its own right: RLVR on verifiable rewards is what trains reasoning ability, not just manners.
Knowledge is frozen at the training cutoff; anything newer must arrive via retrieval or context, not the weights.

concepts.label: Scaling Laws
concepts.summary: Model quality improves as a predictable power law in parameters, data, and compute — the empirical result that justified spending billions on bigger models.
concepts.explanation: Scaling laws are the reason the industry bet so heavily on making models larger. Kaplan et al. found in 2020 that a language model's loss falls as a smooth power law in three quantities — the number of parameters, the size of the training dataset, and the compute spent — with the trend holding across many orders of magnitude. That predictability changed model development from guesswork into planning: you could estimate the capability of a model before training it, and justify the expense. Hoffmann et al.'s 2022 'Chinchilla' work then corrected an influential mistake in how that budget was being spent, showing that models of the day were badly undertrained — for compute-optimal training, parameters and training tokens should scale roughly together, so a smaller model trained on far more data beats a larger, data-starved one. This is why model sizes stopped simply ballooning and training sets exploded instead. More recently the field has added a second axis, inference-time scaling: spending more compute at answer time, by letting a model think for longer, buys accuracy much as training-time scale does — the principle underneath reasoning models.
keyPoints: Kaplan et al. (2020): loss falls as a smooth power law in parameters, data and compute — predictable across many orders of magnitude.
This made capability forecastable before training, which is what justified enormous capital spending on frontier runs.
Chinchilla (Hoffmann et al., 2022) showed models were undertrained: for a fixed compute budget, scale parameters and tokens together — smaller model, far more data.
Inference-time scaling is the newer axis: spending more compute at answer time (thinking longer) also buys accuracy, which is the basis of reasoning models.

concepts.label: KV Cache & PagedAttention
concepts.summary: An inference optimisation that stores past tokens' keys and values so each new token is cheap to generate — memory traded for speed.
concepts.explanation: LLM inference happens in two phases: a parallel 'prefill' that processes the whole prompt at once, and a token-by-token 'decode' that generates the answer. Without help, every new token during decode would recompute attention against all previous tokens, which is enormously wasteful. The KV cache fixes this by storing the keys and values of every token already processed, so generating the next token only requires computing its own query — trading GPU memory for a large speed-up. The problem is that a naive cache reserves a big fixed block of memory per request and wastes much of it to fragmentation. PagedAttention, introduced by the vLLM serving engine, manages the cache like operating-system virtual memory: it splits it into small pages tracked by a block table, so many requests share memory efficiently and total throughput rises sharply. Related tricks build on this — prefix caching reuses a shared prompt across requests, chunked prefill smooths latency, and speculative decoding drafts several tokens with a small model and verifies them with the large one.
keyPoints: LLM inference has two phases: a parallel prefill of the prompt, then token-by-token decode. The cache makes decode cheap by reusing past keys/values.
Naive cache allocation reserves a fixed block per request and wastes GPU memory through fragmentation.
PagedAttention (from vLLM) manages the cache like virtual memory — small pages via a block table — so many requests share memory efficiently and throughput rises.

concepts.label: Prompt Caching
concepts.summary: Caching the processed form of a long, reused prompt prefix so the model skips re-encoding it on every call.
concepts.explanation: When you send the same long prefix to a model repeatedly — a big system prompt, a reference document, a set of few-shot examples — re-encoding it every time is pure waste. Prompt caching stores the internal KV representation produced during the prefill phase for that prefix, so identical content reuses the earlier work instead of being processed again, cutting both latency and cost. It caches the model's internal state, not its final answer, which is a distinct idea from ordinary output caching. What gets reused is decided by prefix matching: the cache is valid only up to the first token that differs, so anything stable must appear at the very start of the prompt and anything variable (like the user's actual question) at the end. There is usually a minimum cacheable size and an expiration window, and some providers offer explicit rather than automatic caching. The practical upshot is a prompt-ordering discipline: put shared, unchanging context first.
keyPoints: It caches the KV pairs from the prefill phase, not the model's output — the same prefix produces the same internal state, so that work is reused.
Prefix matching decides what to reuse: the cache hits only up to the first token that differs, so stable content must come first in the prompt.
It pays off most with long context reused across many requests; there is usually a minimum cacheable size and an expiration window.
Practical impact: put system prompts and shared documents at the top of the prompt, and keep the variable part (the user's question) at the end.

concepts.label: Mixture of Experts
concepts.summary: Grow a model's parameter count without paying to run all of it per token: a router activates only a few 'expert' sub-networks at a time.
concepts.explanation: There is a tension in scaling models: more parameters generally means more capability, but also more compute for every token. Mixture of Experts breaks that link. The network contains many parallel 'expert' sub-networks, and for each token a small router (or gating network) selects just the top few experts to actually run. As a result, the model's total parameter count can be enormous while the active parameters — the ones that determine per-token compute cost — stay modest. This is a major reason frontier models can be both very large and reasonably fast to serve. The experts tend to specialise, though not always in ways humans can interpret. The trade-off is added routing complexity and a memory cost, since all experts must be held in memory even though only a fraction fire on any given token.
keyPoints: A gating/router network selects the top-k experts for each token, so total parameters can be huge while active parameters (the compute cost) stay modest.
This decouples capacity from inference cost — a big reason frontier models can be both very large and reasonably fast.
Experts tend to specialise, though not always in human-interpretable ways.
The trade-off is routing complexity and memory: all experts must be held in memory even though only a few run per token.

concepts.label: Reasoning Models & Chain-of-Thought
concepts.summary: Models trained to spend extra tokens 'thinking' before answering, which measurably improves hard multi-step problems.
concepts.explanation: A plain LLM commits to an answer immediately, which hurts it on problems that need several steps. Chain-of-thought prompting improves this by asking the model to write out its intermediate reasoning before the final answer, and on maths, logic, and multi-step tasks this reliably raises accuracy. Large reasoning models bake the behaviour in: they are trained to produce this deliberation automatically and to allocate a variable 'step budget' of extra inference compute to harder questions. The mechanism that trains it is reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards (RLVR) — the model is rewarded for reaching a checkably correct answer, so useful reasoning strategies like self-checking and backtracking emerge from the reward rather than from anyone labelling the steps. This is also the clearest example of inference-time scaling: thinking longer buys accuracy in the same way that training-time scale does. An important caveat is that the written chain is not a faithful readout of the model's internal computation — it can be a plausible-sounding, post-hoc rationalisation — so you cannot literally 'watch it think', even though the extra tokens help. Because more thinking tokens cost more latency and money, reasoning effort is a dial you tune to the difficulty of the task.
keyPoints: Chain-of-thought prompts the model to lay out intermediate reasoning, which improves accuracy on maths, logic and multi-step tasks.
Large reasoning models are trained to do this automatically and allocate a 'step budget' of extra inference compute to harder questions.

concepts.label: Multimodal Models (VLMs)
concepts.summary: Models that take images, audio, or video alongside text by projecting every modality into the same embedding space the language model already reasons in.
concepts.explanation: Frontier assistants are no longer text-only: they read screenshots, diagrams, documents, and video. The trick that makes this work is that a Transformer does not actually care whether its input vectors came from words. An image is cut into patches, each patch is encoded into a vector, and those vectors are projected into the same embedding space as text tokens — so the language model can attend across words and pixels together with the exact same attention machinery. CLIP established the foundation by training an image encoder and a text encoder jointly on 400 million image-caption pairs, so that a picture of a dog and the phrase 'a photo of a dog' land near each other; that shared space is what lets images be described in language at all. Flamingo and its successors then wired a vision encoder into a pretrained LLM so it could converse about what it sees. Note the direction of travel: this is multimodal *understanding*, the input side, and it complements diffusion, which handles generation on the output side. The practical catch is cost — images consume a surprising number of tokens from the same context window everything else shares.
keyPoints: Images are split into patches, encoded as vectors, and projected into the same embedding space as text — so one Transformer attends over both.
CLIP trained image and text encoders jointly on 400M captioned images, creating the shared space that links pictures to language.
Flamingo-style models connect a vision encoder to a pretrained LLM, giving it the ability to discuss what it sees.
This is the understanding (input) side of multimodality; diffusion covers the generation (output) side. Images are token-expensive and share the same context window.

concepts.label: Diffusion Models
concepts.summary: The generative approach behind most image and video models: learn to remove noise, then denoise from scratch guided by a prompt.
concepts.explanation: Diffusion models generate images and video through a strikingly different mechanism from language models. During training, they take real images and progressively add Gaussian noise until each is pure static, and the network learns to reverse a single step of that corruption. To generate something new, the process runs backwards: start from random noise and repeatedly denoise it, at each step nudging the image toward something coherent and, crucially, toward the meaning of a text prompt. That text conditioning is supplied as an embedding, the same 'meaning as a vector' idea used throughout language models, which is what ties vision and language generation together. Unlike an autoregressive LLM that emits one token at a time, a diffusion model refines the entire output at once over many steps. That makes it a genuine peer of the Transformer rather than a variant of it: this branch holds both of the paradigms behind modern generative AI, autoregressive prediction for language and iterative denoising for images. The two are not isolated — modern image models often use a Transformer as the denoising backbone (a diffusion Transformer, or DiT), and they take their text conditioning from the same embedding space multimodal models use.
keyPoints: Forward process: progressively add Gaussian noise to training images until they are static. The model learns to reverse each step.
Generation: begin with random noise and iteratively denoise, conditioned on a text embedding, to produce an image matching the prompt.
Unlike an autoregressive LLM (one token at a time), diffusion refines the whole output over many steps — a peer paradigm, not a Transformer variant.
The two do meet in practice: modern image models often use a Transformer as the denoising backbone (DiT).

concepts.label: Context Window
concepts.summary: The maximum span of tokens a model can attend to at once — its working memory, shared by everything in a single call.
concepts.explanation: The context window is the model's field of view, measured in tokens, and it is one of the most important practical limits to understand. Everything the model can use in a single call has to fit inside it: the system prompt, the running conversation, any retrieved documents, and the answer being generated all count against the same budget. It is the model's only short-term memory — anything outside the window simply does not exist to the model unless it is re-supplied. Larger windows let you paste in more, but they are not a free lunch: attention dilutes as the window fills and cost rises with length, so 'just use a huge context' has real downsides. Because it is the shared bottleneck, an entire ecosystem of techniques exists to manage it well — RAG to fetch only what's relevant, prompt caching to make reuse cheap, context engineering to curate the payload, and agent memory to persist information across calls.
keyPoints: Measured in tokens; both the input and the generated output count against it.
It is the model's only short-term memory — nothing outside the window exists to the model unless re-supplied.

concepts.label: Hallucination
concepts.summary: When a model states something fluent and confident but false — a direct consequence of predicting likely text, not retrieving facts.
concepts.explanation: Hallucination is not a bolted-on defect; it falls straight out of how an LLM works. Because the model is trained to produce statistically likely continuations, a well-formed but false statement can score just as highly as a true one — it has no internal notion of truth, only plausibility. In practice, most hallucinations are really design flaws: asking the model about data it was never given, or feeding it a document set full of contradictions, is an open invitation to invent. The defences all reduce the model's freedom to make things up — grounding it in retrieved sources (RAG), calibrating its expressed confidence to what the evidence actually supports, and inserting a clarification step for vague questions. The organisational danger is 'hallucination laundering', where a confident wrong answer gets pasted into a report or decision and is then treated as established fact.
keyPoints: The model optimises for plausible continuations, so a well-formed wrong answer can score as highly as a right one.
It is often a design flaw, not model stupidity: asking about data the model was never given, or about contradictory documents, invites invention.

concepts.label: Embeddings
concepts.summary: Turning text, images, or code into vectors of numbers that place similar meanings close together in space.
concepts.explanation: An embedding is how a machine represents meaning as geometry. An embedding model maps a piece of input — a sentence, a document, an image, a code snippet — to a fixed-length vector of numbers, arranged so that things with similar meaning land close together and unrelated things land far apart. This is powerful because it captures meaning rather than surface wording: 'car' and 'automobile' share no letters yet sit near each other, which is exactly what makes semantic search possible. Closeness is quantified with a similarity measure — cosine similarity, dot product, or Euclidean distance — and vectors are often L2-normalised first so only their direction matters. A distinction worth knowing: static embeddings assign one fixed vector per word, while the contextual embeddings produced by Transformers give a word a different vector depending on the sentence it appears in.
keyPoints: An embedding model maps input to a fixed-length vector; distance between vectors reflects semantic similarity, not surface wording.
Two documents that share no keywords ('car' vs 'automobile') can sit close together, which is what makes semantic search possible.

concepts.label: Vector Databases (ANN, HNSW)
concepts.summary: A database that stores embeddings and finds the nearest vectors to a query fast, using approximate nearest-neighbour indexes.
concepts.explanation: Once you can turn text into embedding vectors, you need somewhere to store millions of them and a way to find the closest ones to a query quickly — that is what a vector database does. At query time it embeds the query into the same space and returns the stored vectors nearest to it, which is the mechanical heart of semantic search. The catch is scale: exact nearest-neighbour search compares the query against every stored vector, which is linear in the collection size and far too slow for large corpora. Vector databases therefore use approximate nearest neighbour (ANN) indexes that trade a small amount of accuracy for a huge speed gain. HNSW builds a navigable small-world graph that can be traversed quickly toward the nearest points; IVF partitions the space into clusters and searches only the most promising ones. Tuning knobs (ef_search for HNSW, nprobe for IVF) and quantisation let you trade recall against speed and memory, and the recall@k metric tells you how many of the true nearest neighbours you actually found.
keyPoints: The query is embedded into the same space, then the DB returns the closest stored vectors by similarity — the 'semantic search' step.
Exact nearest-neighbour search is O(n) per query and does not scale; approximate nearest neighbour (ANN) trades a little accuracy for large speed-ups.
HNSW builds a navigable small-world graph for fast traversal; IVF partitions the space into clusters and searches only the nearest ones.
Tuning knobs (ef_search, nprobe) and quantisation trade recall against speed and memory; recall@k measures how many true neighbours you found.

concepts.label: Semantic vs Lexical Search
concepts.summary: Two ways to find relevant documents — matching words versus matching meaning — best combined as hybrid retrieval.
concepts.explanation: There are two fundamentally different ways to find relevant documents, and mature systems use both. Lexical search matches words: techniques like inverted indices, TF-IDF, and BM25 rank documents by keyword overlap, which is fast, precise, and unbeatable for exact terms like names, product codes, or error strings. Semantic search matches meaning: it embeds the query and the documents and compares their vectors, so it catches paraphrases and synonyms that share no words with the query. Each approach fails exactly where the other excels — lexical misses 'automobile' when you searched 'car', while semantic can drift on a precise identifier. Hybrid retrieval fuses their rankings, often with a method like Reciprocal Rank Fusion, to get both precision and recall. A reranker can then take the combined shortlist and reorder it by reading the query and each document together for a final boost in quality.
keyPoints: Lexical search (inverted indices, TF-IDF, BM25) ranks by keyword overlap — great for names, codes and exact phrases.
Semantic search embeds query and documents and compares vectors, catching paraphrases and synonyms lexical search misses.

concepts.label: Retrieval-Augmented Generation
concepts.summary: Give a model knowledge it never learned by retrieving relevant documents at query time and adding them to the prompt.
concepts.explanation: Retrieval-augmented generation is the standard way to make an LLM answer about knowledge it was never trained on — your private documents, or facts newer than its training cutoff. The pattern is three steps: retrieve documents relevant to the question (usually by embedding similarity in a vector database), augment the prompt by inserting that retrieved text, and generate an answer grounded in it rather than in the model's memory alone. This directly patches the two biggest gaps of a bare LLM: stale knowledge and no access to proprietary data. To make retrieval precise, documents are chunked into passages before indexing, so the system fetches focused snippets instead of whole files. The costs are real — per-query latency and a permanent retrieval stack to maintain — and there is a subtle failure mode called silent failure, where retrieval quietly returns the wrong passage and the model answers confidently on top of it. RAG is one of three main customisation strategies, sitting alongside fine-tuning and prompt engineering, and it competes with simply using a very long context window.
keyPoints: Three steps: retrieve documents relevant to the question, augment the prompt with them, generate an answer grounded in that text.
It fixes the two big LLM gaps: stale knowledge (frozen at training cutoff) and no access to your private data.
Documents are chunked before indexing so retrieval returns focused passages, not whole files.
The cost is per-query latency and permanent retrieval infrastructure — and a 'silent failure' mode where retrieval returns the wrong passage and the model answers confidently anyway.

concepts.label: Chunking & Grounding
concepts.summary: Chunking splits documents into retrievable passages; grounding ties the model's answer to those passages so claims are traceable.
concepts.explanation: Two RAG fundamentals live here. Chunking is the preprocessing step of splitting documents into passages small enough to retrieve precisely and to fit inside the context window. Chunk size is a genuine tuning decision: chunks that are too large retrieve imprecisely and waste context, while chunks that are too small lose the surrounding meaning that makes a passage useful — good chunking respects the document's natural structure (sections, paragraphs) rather than cutting blindly at a fixed length. Grounding is the payoff of doing retrieval at all: the model's answer is tied to the specific passages that were retrieved, so each claim can be traced back to a source and checked. That traceability is what lets a RAG system cite its evidence, and grounding is the primary defence against hallucination, because an answer anchored to supplied text has far less room to invent.
keyPoints: Chunk too large and retrieval is imprecise and wastes context; chunk too small and you lose the surrounding meaning — chunk size is a real tuning decision.
Grounding means the answer is supported by supplied text, which is what lets a system cite sources and be checked.
Good chunking respects document structure (sections, paragraphs) rather than cutting blindly at a fixed length.
Grounding is the main defence against hallucination in a RAG system.

concepts.label: Reranking
concepts.summary: A second-stage filter that reads each candidate together with the query and reorders them by true relevance.
concepts.explanation: Retrieval and reranking optimise for different things, and a good pipeline uses them in sequence. The first-stage retriever is built for recall and speed: it uses a bi-encoder that embeds the query and every document separately, so it can search millions of vectors quickly and return a broad set of rough candidates without missing much. The reranker then optimises for precision: it takes that shortlist and, for each candidate, processes the query and the document jointly with a cross-encoder, which reads them together and judges true relevance far more accurately — but is too slow to run over the whole corpus, which is why it only sees the shortlist. Reranking is a defining part of 'advanced RAG', alongside query rewriting and hybrid retrieval, and it directly attacks the silent-failure problem where the right passage was retrieved but ranked too low for the model to use.
keyPoints: Retrieval optimises for recall (don't miss anything) and speed; reranking optimises for precision (put the truly relevant first).
A bi-encoder embeds query and documents separately for fast search; a cross-encoder reranker processes them jointly for accuracy but is slower, so it runs only on the shortlist.

concepts.label: RAG's Evolution
concepts.summary: Retrieval grew from keyword to semantic to hybrid, and RAG grew from a fixed pipeline to a tool inside a reasoning loop.
concepts.explanation: Retrieval-augmented generation did not arrive fully formed; it evolved along two tracks. On the search side, retrieval progressed from keyword matching (inverted indices, BM25) to semantic search over embeddings to hybrid approaches that combine both. On the RAG side, the architecture matured through three stages. Naive RAG is a straight line — embed the question, retrieve the top-k passages, stuff them into the prompt, and generate — with no way to recover if retrieval is poor. Advanced RAG improves the quality of what reaches the model by adding rerankers, query rewriting, and hybrid retrieval. Agentic RAG goes furthest, turning retrieval into a tool the model can call repeatedly, letting it reformulate the query, search again, and reason across multiple hops. That last stage is the bridge from the retrieval branch to the agents branch: it is the same LLM, now deciding for itself when and how to fetch.
keyPoints: Naive RAG is a straight line: embed the question, retrieve top-k, stuff into the prompt, generate — one shot, no recovery if retrieval is poor.
Advanced RAG adds rerankers, query rewriting and hybrid retrieval to raise the quality of what reaches the model.

concepts.label: Long Context vs RAG
concepts.summary: As context windows grew enormously, pasting everything in became a real alternative to retrieval — with genuine trade-offs.
concepts.explanation: Context windows have grown by orders of magnitude, which raises a real question: instead of building a retrieval system, why not just paste the whole document set into the prompt? Long context is genuinely appealing — there is no retrieval stack to build, no chunking to tune, and the model can reason about what is absent from a document because it sees all of it at once. But it has two costs that don't go away: you re-read, and pay for, the entire context on every single query, and attention dilutes as the window fills, so the model's ability to pull out one specific fact can drop (the needle-in-a-haystack problem). RAG, by contrast, scales to an effectively unlimited corpus and only pays to read what it retrieves, at the price of a retrieval stack that can silently fetch the wrong thing. The rule of thumb: reach for long context when the document set is bounded and reused, and for RAG when the knowledge base is large or constantly growing. Prompt caching narrows long context's cost disadvantage considerably.
keyPoints: Long context is simple — no retrieval stack, no chunking, and the model can reason about what is absent from a whole document.

concepts.label: Attention Dilution
concepts.summary: As you cram more into the context window, attention spreads thinner and a specific fact can get lost — the needle in a haystack.
concepts.explanation: Attention dilution is the reason 'just use a bigger context window' does not automatically mean better answers. A model's attention is a finite budget spread across all the tokens in the window, so the more tokens you add, the less focus each one receives on average — and a single crucial fact buried in a very long context can effectively get lost. This is measured by the needle-in-a-haystack test, which checks whether a model can still retrieve one planted fact from a large context; multi-needle variants raise the difficulty by planting several. The phenomenon is a core argument in favour of retrieval: by fetching only a handful of genuinely relevant passages, RAG keeps the model's attention concentrated where it matters instead of asking it to find a needle in an ever-larger haystack.
keyPoints: Attention weight is a finite budget shared across all tokens; more tokens means each gets less focus on average.
The needle-in-a-haystack test measures whether a model can still retrieve one planted fact from a very long context; multi-needle tests raise the bar.
This is a core argument for RAG: retrieving a few relevant passages keeps the model's attention concentrated where it matters.

concepts.label: Why RAG Fails
concepts.summary: Real document sets accumulate contradictions and stale versions, and vague questions make naive RAG return wrong context confidently.
concepts.explanation: RAG works beautifully in demos and then disappoints on real corpora, and the reasons are instructive. Real document sets are messy — they accumulate contradictions and superseded versions over time — so the very same question can have two 'correct' answers depending on which document retrieval happens to surface, and a naive pipeline has no idea which is authoritative. On top of that, users ask underspecified questions, and the system answers them literally. The fixes are practical rather than magical. First, keep stale documents out of the index using supersession metadata, so retrieval physically cannot surface them — letting them in is an unforced error. Second, add a clarification loop that catches vague or ambiguous questions before answering. Third, calibrate the model's confidence to what the retrieved data actually supports, so it hedges when the evidence is thin. The underlying lesson is that you must know your data before you build, because in most of these cases the 'hallucination' is really a design flaw.
keyPoints: The same question can have two correct answers if the corpus contains superseded and current documents both — retrieval has no idea which is authoritative.
Fix 1: keep stale documents out of the index (supersession metadata) so retrieval cannot surface them — an 'unforced error' if you don't.
Fix 2: add a clarification loop to catch vague or ambiguous questions before answering.
Fix 3: calibrate the model's confidence to what the retrieved data actually supports — and know your data before you build, because 'hallucination' here is usually a design flaw.

concepts.label: Grounding
concepts.summary: Anchoring a model's output in verifiable source material so claims can be traced and trusted.
concepts.explanation: Grounding is the property that separates a citable assistant from a plausible talker. A grounded answer is one whose claims point back to specific source passages that support them, so a reader can trace and verify each statement rather than taking the model's word for it. Ungrounded generation, by contrast, relies purely on the model's parametric memory — the knowledge baked into its weights — which is precisely where hallucination lives. Grounding is the shared goal that several retrieval techniques serve: retrieval supplies the sources, chunking makes them precise, and confidence calibration keeps the model from over-claiming beyond what those sources say. In short, grounding is what turns raw generative fluency into something an organisation can actually rely on.
keyPoints: A grounded answer points back to the passages that support it, making it checkable.

concepts.label: Prompt Engineering
concepts.summary: The cheapest way to steer a model: change what you ask, aiming its attention at capability it already has.
concepts.explanation: Prompt engineering is the first and cheapest lever for improving an LLM's output, because it changes the request rather than the model. A well-constructed prompt gives clear instructions, useful structure, and often worked examples — few-shot prompting includes several input-output examples so the model infers the pattern you want. The important mental model is that prompting unlocks capability the model already possesses; it aims the model's attention at latent skill, but it cannot add knowledge the model never learned or grant access to your private data. That is why it is the right thing to try first: it is instant and essentially free compared with standing up a retrieval system or running a fine-tune. And when prompting stops yielding improvements — when you've phrased the task as clearly as it can be phrased and results have plateaued — that plateau is the signal to move up to context engineering, RAG, or fine-tuning.
keyPoints: Few-shot prompting includes worked examples in the prompt so the model infers the pattern you want.

concepts.label: Context Engineering
concepts.summary: Deciding exactly what goes into the context window on each call — instructions, tools, retrieved data, memory — and in what order.
concepts.explanation: Context engineering is what prompt engineering grew into once models gained tools, memory, and retrieval. Where prompt engineering is about wording a single instruction, context engineering is about assembling the entire payload that goes into the context window on each call — which instructions, which tool definitions, which retrieved documents, which pieces of past interaction — and arranging them in the right order. It matters because the model can only reason over what you actually put in the window; the best information in the world is useless if it isn't there, and irrelevant filler actively hurts by diluting attention. This is the umbrella discipline that ties together several other ideas on this map: RAG decides which documents to include, agent memory decides which history to recall, skills decide which procedures to load, and prompt caching decides how to make reused context cheap. Done well, it is the single highest-leverage form of tuning available short of changing the model.

concepts.label: Fine-Tuning
concepts.summary: Change the model itself by continuing training on a narrow dataset, so a style, format, or domain becomes part of the weights.
concepts.explanation: Fine-tuning is the heaviest customisation lever: instead of changing the prompt or the context, you change the model. You continue the training process on a curated, narrow dataset, and backpropagation actually moves the weights so the desired behaviour — a house style, a strict output format, a specialised domain — becomes internalised rather than instructed. The power comes with recurring costs that are easy to underestimate: preparing high-quality training data, paying for GPUs, and re-tuning as the base model keeps improving underneath you, plus the risk of catastrophic forgetting, where teaching the model something new erodes abilities it already had. Fine-tuning genuinely shines in a few places: durable style or format, narrow domains, low-latency needs (no retrieval step at inference), and distilling a big model's behaviour into a smaller, cheaper one. But the practical decision order is to exhaust prompt engineering and context/RAG first, and fine-tune only when those plateau — because general models keep catching up to yesterday's fine-tunes.

concepts.label: LoRA & PEFT
concepts.summary: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning: train a small number of added weights instead of all of them, cutting cost by orders of magnitude.
concepts.explanation: Full fine-tuning updates every weight in a model, which needs a lot of memory and compute and produces a whole new copy of the model per task. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) avoids this by freezing the base model and training only a small set of added parameters. LoRA, the most popular PEFT method, inserts tiny low-rank adapter matrices alongside the existing weights and trains only those; a single number called the rank (r) controls how much capacity the adapter has. Because the adapters are small, you get two big wins: training is far cheaper in memory and compute, and you can keep many task-specific adapters for one shared base model instead of many full copies. Related advanced techniques in the same family include distillation, which trains a small model to imitate a large one, and reinforcement fine-tuning, which optimises against a grader that scores the model's outputs.
keyPoints: PEFT freezes the base model and trains only a small set of added parameters, so you need far less memory and compute.

concepts.label: Synthetic Data
concepts.summary: When you lack labelled data to customise a model, generate it — then validate it before you trust it.
concepts.explanation: Customising a model often stalls on a shortage of good training data, and synthetic data generation is the workaround: you manufacture the examples you need. It starts with extraction, because you can't just point a model at a raw PDF — documents must first be parsed into clean, structured context using OCR and tools like Docling. From a small set of seed examples, a generator then produces many more synthetic samples that match the shape and distribution you want. The non-negotiable step is validation: synthetic data must be checked for faithfulness, relevance, and diversity before it is used, or you risk training the model on its own errors and amplifying them. The reward for doing this well is control — you can deliberately balance classes, protect privacy by not using real records, and get reproducibility that scraped or found data can never offer.

concepts.label: AI Evaluation
concepts.summary: The systematic measurement of whether your AI system is actually good — and the only thing that turns changing a prompt from guesswork into engineering.
concepts.explanation:
Because a language model produces fluent output whether or not that output is correct, 'is this good?' cannot be answered by reading a couple of responses and feeling reassured. Evaluation is the instrument panel you steer by: a fixed set of measurements you re-run after every change, so you can tell whether you improved the system or quietly broke a case you were not looking at.

The practice is less glamorous than it sounds. It starts with a human reading model outputs one at a time in a spreadsheet, grading them against written criteria, and arguing with a teammate about the borderline ones. Everything automated is built on top of that: you encode the criteria as a judge prompt, check that the judge agrees with your humans, and only then trust it at scale. Skip the human step and you get metrics that look rigorous and measure nothing.

The classic machine-learning version of this — hold out a test set, score with accuracy, precision/recall, F1, recall@k — still applies wherever a single correct answer exists. Generative output usually has no single correct answer, which is why the branch below is mostly about how to measure quality when you cannot simply diff against a reference. Throughout, the hazard is Goodhart's Law: once a metric becomes the target it stops being a good metric, so measure what you actually care about rather than whatever is easiest to count.
keyPoints: An eval is a systematic measurement of one specific aspect of quality; a real system has many of them, not one overall score.
The purpose is regression safety: a fixed set of cases you re-run so 'I fixed it' becomes 'I fixed it and nothing else broke'.
Everything automated is built on hand-labelled human judgement — that foundation determines the ceiling of everything above it.
Classic ML metrics (accuracy, precision/recall, F1, recall@k) apply where one correct answer exists; generative output needs judges and rubrics.
Evals are operationalised three ways: background monitoring, real-time guardrails, and improvement tooling for labelling and datasets.
Beware Goodhart's Law: once a metric becomes the target it stops being a good metric.

concepts.label: The Four Types of Eval
concepts.summary: Code-based, human, LLM-as-a-judge, and user evals — a ladder from cheap and narrow to expensive and real, where each level is validated by the one below it.
concepts.explanation:
Essentially every evaluation falls into one of four buckets, and naming which one you are reaching for stops you from using an expensive tool on a cheap problem.

Code-based evals are deterministic pass/fail assertions: checking for the presence of a string, validating a format, confirming a field holds an allowed value. They are level zero, nearly free, and fast to write. The canonical case is a competitor check — if you are United, a reply explaining how to book on Delta is a failure a substring match catches, with no judgement required.

Human evals are a person, ideally the product owner or a domain expert, reading an interaction and grading it. This is the slowest and most expensive form per example, and it is also the only one that defines what 'good' means in the first place. LLM-as-a-judge scales that judgement by having a model apply the same rubric, and is the most common way to evaluate at volume. User evals are the closest thing to a business metric: real feedback from real people, from an explicit thumbs-down to a downstream conversion number.

The ordering matters more than the list. Each level is validated by the one before it — the judge is trustworthy only because humans checked it, and human labels are meaningful only because someone defined criteria worth grading against.
keyPoints: Code-based: deterministic pass/fail assertions — string presence, format checks, allowed values. Cheap and unambiguous.
Human: a product owner or domain expert grading by hand. Slowest per example, and the source of truth for everything else.
LLM-as-a-judge: a model applying your rubric at scale, imitating how a human would label.
User: real-world signal from actual users — thumbs up/down, complaints, downstream business metrics.
Do not fully outsource human eval to contractors: whoever owns the product judgement has to be in the spreadsheet.

concepts.label: Rubrics & Criteria
concepts.summary: Turning 'is this good?' into named dimensions with written definitions, so two people grading the same output reach the same label for the same reason.
concepts.explanation:
A rubric is the bridge between a vague sense of quality and a number you can act on. Rather than grading an output as good or bad overall, you name the dimensions that matter for your product and grade each separately.

For a customer-support agent, three dimensions fall out of what can go wrong: product knowledge (does it actually know the catalogue?), policy compliance (is it following the rules it was given?), and tone (does it sound the way this brand should?). Each is graded good, average, or bad — and each grade needs a written definition, so that 'average tone' means the same thing to everyone.

Splitting the dimensions apart is what makes a rubric diagnostic. One overall score tells you the output was bad; three dimensions tell you it was bad because it violated policy while its product knowledge was fine — and those two failures have completely different fixes. Writing the rubric before labelling begins matters too, because criteria invented mid-grading drift as you go.

Expect the rubric to evolve anyway. As you see more data you discover that what you care about is more specific than what you first wrote down, and refining the criterion is a normal part of the process rather than evidence you got it wrong.
keyPoints: Name dimensions rather than grading one overall 'good' — for a support agent: product knowledge, policy compliance, tone.
Write explicit definitions of good/average/bad per dimension so labels are consistent between people.
Separate dimensions are diagnostic: they point at which part of the system to fix.
Write the rubric before labelling starts; one invented while grading drifts.
Criteria legitimately shift as you see more data — refinement is expected, not a failure.

concepts.label: Golden Datasets
concepts.summary: A hand-labelled set of real examples that serves as the reference standard — the foundation every automated eval inherits its quality from.
concepts.explanation:
The golden dataset is a table: one row per interaction, columns for the input, the system's output, a grade per rubric dimension, and a free-text note. You build it by running real questions through your system and grading what comes back. That is the whole technique, and a spreadsheet is genuinely the right tool.

What makes the tedium worth it is that grading forces specificity. A single row — a customer inside the return window who has thrown away the box, answered correctly on the policy but without ever giving contact details — surfaces both a product decision nobody had made and a gap in the policy document itself. Neither is found by reading the answer casually and nodding.

Size follows the weight of the decision. About ten rows is enough for internal iteration and for checking whether an approach is worth pursuing; a hundred or more before you trust a number for a production decision, and considerably more in a regulated domain. It is fundamentally a statistics question. The reason not to start at a hundred is that confidence and iteration speed pull against each other: more data means a more trustworthy number and a slower loop, and early on you are changing the prompt constantly.

Real captured inputs are best. If you do not have a hundred yet, LLM-generated synthetic examples are a legitimate way to start — provided you validate them before trusting them.
keyPoints: One row per interaction: input, output, a grade per dimension, and a note. The notes are where the value accumulates.
Grading forces the team to settle product decisions the specification left open — the debate is the point.
About 10 rows for internal iteration; 100+ before trusting a production decision; more in regulated domains.
Confidence and iteration speed are orthogonal — pick your position deliberately and revisit it as the product matures.
Real captured examples are best; validated synthetic data is a legitimate way to bootstrap.

concepts.label: LLM-as-a-Judge
concepts.summary: Using a strong model to apply your rubric at scale — the only practical way to evaluate thousands of open-ended outputs, and useless until you prove it agrees with humans.
concepts.explanation:
Once you have a rubric and hand-labelled examples you trust, you can scale. An LLM judge is a second model whose job is to apply your criteria to your system's outputs and emit a label, exactly as a human labeller would.

The judge prompt is not a new artefact — it is the rubric you already wrote, addressed to a model, with the same context a human grader had. Run one judge per dimension so each call makes a single focused judgement, and use the most capable model you can afford; this is not the job for a cheap small model.

The non-negotiable detail is that the judge must produce an explanation alongside its label. The explanation plays the role a human reviewer's notes play: it lets you read why the judge scored something as it did and decide whether you agree with the reasoning. A bare score is unauditable — you cannot distinguish a correct judgement from a lucky one.

What this buys is reference-free evaluation: judging qualities like 'is this natural?' or 'does this sound human?' where no gold answer exists and word-overlap metrics say nothing. The cost is that the judge is itself a fallible language model, with systematic biases and a real chance of being confidently miscalibrated — which is why the alignment step below is not optional.
keyPoints: The judge prompt is your rubric restated as model instructions, given the same context the human grader had.
Run one judge per dimension, and use the strongest model you can afford.

concepts.label: Direct Assessment vs Pairwise
concepts.summary: Score each output against a rubric, or ask which of two is better — an absolute standard versus a relative comparison, often best combined.
concepts.explanation:
There are two ways to put a judge to work, and they answer different questions.

Direct assessment scores each output independently against a rubric you designed: is this summary clear and coherent — yes or no? Its strengths are control and interpretability. You wrote the criterion, the resulting label means something standalone, and labels aggregate naturally into a pass rate. That makes it the natural fit for compliance-style questions where the requirement is fixed and external.

Pairwise comparison shows the judge two outputs and asks which is better. Relative judgements are easier and more consistent than absolute ones for subjective qualities, because the judge need not locate a threshold that may not exist. With more than two candidates, a ranking algorithm converts accumulated pairwise verdicts into an overall ordering. The limitation is that a win is purely relative — 'A beat B' says nothing about whether either was acceptable.

IBM's user research on its open-sourced EvalAssist framework found roughly half of participants preferred direct assessment for its clarity and rubric control, about a quarter preferred pairwise for subjective tasks, and the remainder combined the two: direct assessment as a compliance gate, then pairwise ranking to select the best of what passed. That combined pattern resolves the trade-off rather than picking a side, giving you an absolute quality floor and a relative ordering above it. The overall conclusion was that the choice is both task- and user-dependent.
keyPoints: Direct assessment: score each output independently against a rubric. Clear, controllable, aggregates into a pass rate.
Pairwise comparison: ask which of two outputs is better. Easier and more consistent for subjective qualities.
A ranking algorithm turns many pairwise verdicts into an overall ordering of all candidates.
A pairwise win is relative — it does not tell you whether either output met your bar.
EvalAssist user research: ~half preferred direct assessment, ~a quarter pairwise (especially for subjective tasks), the rest combined both.
The combined pipeline — direct assessment as a gate, then pairwise ranking — gives a quality floor plus an ordering.

concepts.label: Judge Biases
concepts.summary: Positional, verbosity, and self-enhancement bias make a judge favour outputs for reasons unrelated to quality — systematically, so they do not average out.
concepts.explanation:
Like human reviewers, LLM judges have blind spots, and they show up as systematic biases: errors that lean consistently in one direction rather than cancelling out across a large sample. This is why more data produces a more confident wrong answer rather than convergence on the truth.

Positional bias is a preference tied to where an output appears. In a pairwise comparison, a judge exhibiting it keeps choosing option A regardless of what is in option A — the judgement is driven by slot rather than substance. Verbosity bias is the judge treating length as a proxy for quality, favouring the longer answer even when it is repetitive or wanders; the model reads length as thoroughness, which is precisely the wrong instinct in a system meant to reward clarity. Self-enhancement bias is a judge rating output it recognises as its own more highly, independent of whether the content is better.

Positional bias has a clean, cheap test: run the comparison twice with the options swapped. A judge evaluating content picks the same output both times and the winner merely changes slot; a positionally biased judge keeps picking its preferred slot, so the verdict flips. Per pair, a flip marks that comparison unreliable; in aggregate, the flip rate quantifies how biased the judge is on your task.

The method generalises. For any suspected bias, construct a variation that changes only the suspect factor while holding content constant — swap order to test position, pad an answer with harmless filler to test verbosity, strip model identifiers to test self-enhancement — and see whether the verdict moves. Bias does not mean the system is broken; it means you stay vigilant, and good frameworks build these checks in.
keyPoints: Positional bias: favouring an output for its position — always picking option A regardless of content.
Verbosity bias: favouring longer output regardless of quality, reading length as thoroughness.
Self-enhancement bias: rating its own generated output more highly than others'.
These skew results systematically rather than adding noise, so they do not average out with more samples.
Positional swaps — re-running with the order reversed — detect positional bias directly; the flip rate quantifies it.
General method: vary only the suspected factor, hold content constant, and check whether the verdict moves.

concepts.label: Judge Alignment & Agreement
concepts.summary: Measuring how often the judge's label matches the human's — the step almost everyone skips, and the one that decides whether any of your metrics mean anything.
concepts.explanation:
This separates evaluation from theatre. In a real session, an LLM judge labelled every single example 'good' — a result that is worthless in a way that looks like success, since a dashboard would show a perfect score. The only reason anyone noticed is that human labels existed to compare against.

The metric goes by two names for the same idea: match rate, or agreement score — the fraction of examples where the judge's label equals the human's, computed per dimension. Per-dimension is what makes it actionable: in the worked example product knowledge matched 100% of the time while tone matched once, which immediately localises the fault to the tone judge rather than the system.

The loop is: hand-label five to ten examples, run the judge on the same ones, compute agreement, read the judge's explanations on the rows that disagree, tighten those judge prompts, and repeat. Crucially the human critique stays fixed — it is the golden standard you are optimising toward, and adjusting human labels to match the model would guarantee agreement while destroying its meaning. Only the judge prompt is a free variable. Meta-prompting is the powerful way to iterate: show a strong model the disagreements, the current agreement score, and the current judge prompt, and ask it to rewrite the prompt to maximise agreement without overfitting to individual rows.

Only once the judge tracks your humans on a small set do you scale it to a hundred examples and start believing the aggregate. And it never fully ends: prompts, data, features, and users drift, so what 'good' means drifts too, and a judge aligned to last quarter's standard quietly stops measuring the current one.
keyPoints: Match rate / agreement score = the fraction of rows where the judge's label equals the human's, computed per dimension.
A judge that labels everything 'good' yields a flawless dashboard and zero information — only human labels expose it.
Per-dimension scores localise the fault: 100% on product knowledge and 20% on tone means the tone judge is broken.
The human critique is the fixed golden standard; only the judge prompt changes.
Meta-prompting — handing a strong model the disagreements and the current judge prompt — is the effective way to iterate.
Validate on 5–10 rows, then scale to 100+. Re-check forever, because drift makes 'good' a moving target.
