concepts.label: The Three Levels of Evals
concepts.summary: Unit tests on every change, human and model review every week, A/B tests on major releases — cost and effort rise with each level, which dictates how often you run it.
concepts.explanation:
Organising evaluation by cost makes it practical, because it tells you what to run when.

Level one is unit tests: fast, cheap assertions run on every code and prompt change. Level two is human and model evaluation — systematic review of quality, run weekly or bi-weekly depending on the size of the system, and costly mainly because humans spend time on it. Level three is A/B testing with real users to measure business impact, reserved for major releases because it needs enough traffic and time to mean anything.

The common mistake is jumping straight to level two's automation without its human half. The tempting picture is plugging in an eval tool, giving an LLM some instructions, and letting it monitor everything — and it is what you should avoid at all cost early on. You cannot write instructions for a review you have not learned to perform yourself. Humans look at data first; the judge is aligned to them afterwards, never the reverse.

The level-three question deserves a cheaper answer than most teams assume. Before wiring user-satisfaction telemetry into your product, you can compare two prompts against your own labelled dataset using the judge you already aligned, and get most of the decision value at a fraction of the cost. Full in-app A/B testing suits mature, high-traffic applications where tiny prompt changes matter.
keyPoints: Level 1 — unit tests: fast, cheap assertions on every code and prompt change.
Level 2 — human and model evaluation: systematic review, weekly or bi-weekly, humans first and judges aligned to them.
Level 3 — A/B testing with real users for business impact, reserved for major releases.
Cost and effort rise with each level, which is what dictates how often each is run.
You cannot skip the human half of level 2: you cannot instruct a model to perform a review you have not learned to do.
Cheaper middle ground: compare prompt variants offline against your labelled set before exposing users.

concepts.label: Unit Tests as Evals
concepts.summary: Ordinary assertions over structured output, run on every change — the cheapest tier, and the one that catches regressions nothing else would.
concepts.explanation:
Level one is ordinary software unit testing applied to an LLM workflow, and it is the tier you run most often because it costs almost nothing.

The mechanism is a plain assertion: the condition must evaluate to true, and a false condition raises an error you can catch and report. The most productive place to apply it is structured output, because structured output gives you fields with types and allowed values you can check deterministically. For a support ticket classifier: assert the category is one of your known categories, the confidence is a float, it lies between 0 and 1, and — specific to this input — the category is billing.

This is why capturing raw events matters so much. Store the exact input payloads your workflow received in an evals folder, and they become your test fixtures: realistic inputs reflecting the messy reality users produce, rather than the happy path you imagined. Every incident you diagnose turns into a permanent regression test. As a workflow grows to five or ten steps, you assert at every step — classification, routing, confidence on the structured object, the generated answer, the success flag from the final API call — so a failure localises to a stage.

What should you test? The failure modes you have actually observed. When something breaks and you diagnose it, write the test that pins it down so it can never recur silently. Start with a simple loop and a printed report; move to a proper test runner when you want one command to run the folder.

Structured output is the natural target: assert allowed values, types, and ranges.
Keep an evals folder of raw event payloads captured from production — they are your test fixtures.
Assert at every step of a multi-step workflow so failures localise to a stage.
What to test comes from observed failure modes: diagnose once, then pin it with a test forever.

concepts.label: A/B Testing & User Evals
concepts.summary: Shipping to real users in stages — dogfood, then a small traffic slice — and reading signals that are genuine but harder to interpret than they look.
concepts.explanation:
Offline evaluation on a golden dataset answers 'does this behave the way we decided it should?' It cannot answer 'do real users get what they came for?' For that you have to ship, carefully.

The progression is internal dogfooding first, which is high-value because the people using it already know what good looks like, then an A/B test on a small traffic slice — on the order of 1% to 10% depending on company size and the risk of the surface — and only then broader rollout. The metrics at this level are business metrics: user satisfaction, task completion rate, time to resolution, engagement, and ultimately sales and retention.

User signals are the most real and the hardest to interpret. Consider a customer who thumbs-downs a reply telling them they are not eligible for a refund. The agent applied the policy correctly, communicated clearly, and did its job; the customer is unhappy about the outcome, not the answer. The signal is genuine but it conflates 'the system performed badly' with 'I did not like the news' — and treating it as a quality failure would train the system to misstate policy in order to please people.

So settle the question before you need it: what do you do when the eval says good and the business metric goes down? There is no formula. In a non-deterministic system you cannot fully trust your users' labels or your own, and the resolution is always the same — go back and read the data.
keyPoints: Sequence: internal dogfooding, then a 1–10% A/B slice, then broader rollout with monitoring.
Level-3 metrics are business metrics: satisfaction, task completion, time to resolution, engagement, retention.
A thumbs-down conflates 'the system did badly' with 'I disliked the outcome' — genuine signal, ambiguous meaning.
Decide in advance how you break the tie when evals look good and the business metric drops.

concepts.label: Reference-Based vs Reference-Free
concepts.summary: When you know the correct answer, testing is easy; when many answers are valid, you score qualities instead — which is where judges become necessary.
concepts.explanation:
Metrics divide into two categories, and knowing which one you are in tells you how hard the measurement will be.

Reference-based metrics apply when a golden answer exists and you can compare against it: exact string matching, semantic similarity, code execution results, SQL correctness, structured data validation. These are comparatively easy, and much of this can be captured as unit tests. The traditional text metrics BLEU and ROUGE also live here — they score an output by how much its wording overlaps a reference. That works for machine translation and breaks down elsewhere: a summary can share most of its vocabulary with the reference and still be incoherent, or share little and be excellent.

Reference-free metrics apply when you do not know exactly what the output should be, or when many outputs are legitimately correct. Answering a customer query has effectively infinite good answers differing in tone, length, and structure. Here you score qualities instead — tone appropriateness, length constraints, absence of hallucination, format compliance, safety and toxicity — usually on a 0–1 or 1–5 scale.

Real systems lean heavily on reference-free metrics, which is exactly why LLM judges and the alignment discipline matter so much: they are the only practical way to measure a quality that no overlap score can reach. Whichever category you are in, the advice is the same: start binary. Good and bad is challenging enough to get right.

concepts.label: Evaluation-Driven Development
concepts.summary: The analyze → measure → improve cycle, and the four mistakes that keep teams stuck at the demo: tool-first thinking, generic metrics, avoiding your data, and unaligned judges.
concepts.explanation:
Three challenges make LLM development different from ordinary software. You do not understand the data flowing through your system, because you tested the happy path and real users are unpredictable. There is a specification gap between what you want and what you can express in a prompt — you know a good output when you see it, but translating that into instructions is hard, and attributing a bad output to prompting, retrieval, or pipeline logic is its own problem. And behaviour is inconsistent: small wording changes produce completely different outputs.

The working loop that addresses all three is analyze → measure → improve, a lifecycle articulated by Hamel Husain and Shreya Shankar. Analyze: collect real examples and categorise the failure modes, which arrive as user complaints, errors you spot while reading data, and outright application errors. Measure: turn those insights into quantitative metrics, starting with booleans. Improve: refine prompts, try different models, change the architecture. Then go round again — running it repeatedly is what creates a flywheel rather than a series of one-off fixes.

Four mistakes recur. Tool-first thinking reaches for a purchase instead of a diagnosis — a new vector database, a bigger model, an eval platform with ten metrics out of the box. Generic-metrics obsession drowns you in unactionable scores like 'helpfulness 4.2'. Avoiding your data is the most consequential, and sounds like 'the LLM will check it' or 'users will tell us if it's broken'. Unaligned judges is assuming the judge works without validating it.

The habit that matters most is unglamorous: look at lots of real data, constantly. Manual inspection has the highest value-to-prestige ratio in the whole discipline. You know you are succeeding when you can deploy changes confidently, failures are caught before users see them, and improvements compound; you are struggling when every fix breaks something else and progress feels like trial and error.

Analyze → measure → improve is the working loop; running it repeatedly is what compounds improvement.

concepts.label: Generative vs Agentic AI
concepts.summary: The difference between one call and a loop: a generative model reacts once; an agent pursues a goal by looping with tools.
concepts.explanation: This is the conceptual dividing line of the whole agents branch. Generative AI is reactive: you send a prompt, it returns output, and it holds no larger objective across calls — one input, one response. Agentic AI is proactive: given a goal, it enters a loop — it perceives the current state, decides on a step, acts by calling a tool, observes the result, and repeats until the goal is met. What makes this possible is that both sit on the same substrate: an LLM acting as the reasoning engine. The agent is not a different kind of model; it is the scaffolding of tools, memory, and control flow built around a generative model to let it act rather than merely answer. The genuinely hard engineering skill is building systems that know when to simply generate a response and when to enter the more expensive, more capable act-and-observe loop.

Agentic AI is proactive: it plans, calls tools, reads the results, and decides the next step, repeating around a loop.

concepts.label: The Agent Loop & Building Blocks
concepts.summary: An agent is the model plus a control loop and a set of parts — instructions, tools, memory, and often sub-agents.

concepts.label: Tool Use & A2A
concepts.summary: Tools are how an agent reaches beyond text to act; agent-to-agent protocols let one agent delegate to another as if it were a tool.
concepts.explanation: Without tools, a model can only talk; tools are what let an agent do things in the world. The mechanism is function calling: the model emits a structured request — say, call get_weather(city='Paris') — the runtime executes that function and returns the result, and the agent incorporates it into its next step. Tools can be anything with an interface: databases, APIs, code execution, file systems. Agent-to-agent (A2A) protocols extend the same idea one level up, defining how autonomous agents discover and invoke each other, so one agent can hand a subtask to another specialised agent as though calling a tool. An 'agent card' advertises what a given agent is able to do so others can find and use it. Delegating to a focused specialist keeps each agent's context tight and lets independent work run in parallel — but every tool an agent can reach also widens the attack surface a defender has to secure.

concepts.label: Model Context Protocol (MCP)
concepts.summary: A standard interface between an LLM and external tools and data — the 'USB-C for AI tools'.
concepts.explanation: Before MCP, every connection between a model and an external system was a bespoke integration, which did not scale as agents multiplied. The Model Context Protocol standardises that connection, so a single integration works across any MCP-aware model — the way USB-C standardised device connectors. An MCP server exposes two things: tools, which are actions the model can invoke, and resources, which are data the model can read, typically communicated over JSON-RPC. Crucially, MCP solves access but not procedure: it gives the model a governed way to reach a tool, but it does not tell the model the repeatable, reliable way to use that tool well — that gap is what agent skills fill. Because it standardises how an agent touches the outside world, MCP shows up wherever an agent needs controlled access to external services, and it is a natural place to enforce security policy.

concepts.label: Agent Skills
concepts.summary: A packaged, reusable procedure the model can auto-load when relevant — the 'how to do X' that MCP's 'access to X' leaves out.

The clever part is auto-loading: the model keeps only the short description in view and pulls the full skill into context only when the current task matches, which conserves the context window instead of carrying every procedure at all times. So the division of labour is clean — MCP provides access to a capability, and a skill provides the repeatable recipe for using that capability well. Conceptually a skill is procedural memory made portable: the same 'how-to' knowledge described in the agent-memory branch, packaged so it can be shared across agents.

concepts.label: Agent Memory (4 Types)
concepts.summary: Agents need memory beyond one context window; the CoALA framework names four kinds — working, semantic, procedural, and episodic.
concepts.explanation: A single context window is not enough memory for an agent that operates over time, so agent architectures borrow a four-part scheme from human cognition, formalised in the CoALA framework. Working memory is what the agent is holding right now — literally the context window. Semantic memory is what the agent knows: facts and documents, usually stored externally and pulled in through retrieval (RAG). Procedural memory is how the agent does things: reusable workflows and skills it can load on demand. Episodic memory is what happened before: records of past interactions the agent can recall to inform present behaviour. Each of the four child nodes below covers one type in depth. Two cross-cutting points matter: forgetting is an engineering problem, since stale entries must be invalidated and memory pruned to stay useful, and not every agent needs all four — a simple reflex agent may need only working memory.

concepts.label: Working Memory
concepts.summary: The agent's short-term memory — literally the context window: fast and immediate, but bounded and wiped between sessions.
concepts.explanation: Working memory is the agent's here-and-now, and in practice it is exactly the model's context window. It holds the current task, the recent messages, and any data freshly retrieved for this step, all immediately available to the model's reasoning. Its defining limitation is that it is both finite and volatile: it can hold only so many tokens, and anything not written out to a durable store disappears when the window rolls over or the session ends. That volatility is the whole reason the other three memory types exist — semantic, procedural, and episodic memory are all ways to persist information beyond a single window and pull it back in when needed. Managing working memory well — deciding what deserves a place in that scarce space at each step — is precisely the context-engineering problem.
keyPoints: It holds the current task, recent messages and freshly retrieved data — everything immediately in play.
It is finite and volatile: anything not written to a durable store is gone when the window rolls over.
Its limits are why semantic, procedural and episodic memory exist as durable stores.
Managing it well is exactly the context-engineering problem.

concepts.label: Semantic Memory
concepts.summary: What the agent knows — facts, documents, and domain knowledge — stored externally and retrieved when relevant.
concepts.explanation: Semantic memory is the agent's store of knowledge: facts, definitions, documentation, and domain information that it can draw on, independent of any particular past conversation. Because this knowledge is far too large to keep permanently in the context window, it lives in an external store and is pulled in on demand — which is exactly what retrieval-augmented generation does, making RAG the usual implementation of semantic memory. When the agent needs a fact, it retrieves the relevant passages and loads them into working memory for that step. The engineering challenge is keeping this knowledge fresh and correct: stale entries have to be invalidated so the agent doesn't reason from outdated information, the same 'know your data' discipline that makes RAG reliable in the first place.

concepts.label: Procedural Memory
concepts.summary: How the agent does things — reusable procedures it can load on demand, kept cheap through progressive disclosure.
concepts.explanation: Procedural memory is the agent's store of 'how to', as distinct from semantic memory's 'what is' — it holds the workflows, routines, and step-by-step methods the agent has learned or been given. Keeping every procedure loaded at all times would flood the context window, so procedural memory uses progressive disclosure: the agent keeps only a lightweight index of available procedures in view and loads the full detail of one only when a task actually calls for it. This is the same mechanism that powers agent skills, which are essentially procedural memory packaged to be portable and shared across agents. By separating the index from the detail, an agent can 'know about' a large library of procedures cheaply while paying the context cost of only the ones it is actively using.
keyPoints: It stores the 'how-to' — the agent's learned or given workflows — rather than facts.
Progressive disclosure indexes many procedures cheaply and loads a full one only when relevant, conserving the context window.

Separating a lightweight index from full detail lets an agent know about many procedures at low cost.

concepts.label: Episodic Memory
concepts.summary: What happened before — records of past interactions the agent recalls to inform how it behaves now.
concepts.explanation: Episodic memory is the agent's record of specific past events: previous conversations, decisions it made, actions it took, and how they turned out. Unlike semantic memory, which stores general facts, episodic memory is tied to particular episodes in time, and recalling a relevant past episode lets the agent behave consistently and learn from experience rather than starting fresh every session. Because these records accumulate, forgetting becomes an explicit engineering concern: an agent that recalls a stale note — an instruction or fact that was true then but is wrong now — can act on outdated information, so scoped invalidation and pruning are needed to keep episodic memory trustworthy. Done well, it is what lets an assistant remember your earlier preferences or pick up a task where it left off.

concepts.label: Agentic Frameworks
concepts.summary: Libraries that coordinate agents, from simple linear workflows to autonomous and role-based multi-agent systems.
concepts.explanation: Once you move past a single agent, you need something to coordinate control flow, tool access, memory, and communication between agents — that is what an agentic framework provides. Frameworks span a spectrum of autonomy, and choosing the right shape means matching it to how much unpredictability your task can tolerate. There are roughly five shapes: linear workflows run fixed, predetermined steps; autonomous multi-agent systems let agents converse and self-organise; role-based multi-agent systems assign agents distinct personas or jobs (a 'crew'); production orchestration systems add the reliability and control needed to run at scale; and rapid-prototyping tools optimise for quick experimentation. concepts.label: Agentic RAG
concepts.summary: Retrieval used as a tool inside a reasoning loop, so the agent decides when to search and gathers evidence across multiple hops.
concepts.explanation: Agentic RAG is where the retrieval branch and the agents branch meet. In naive RAG, retrieval is a fixed step that always runs once before generation; in agentic RAG, retrieval becomes just another tool the agent can choose to call, as often as the problem demands. That shift is powerful: the agent can issue a search, judge whether the results are good enough, rewrite a weak query and search again, and combine findings from several searches to answer multi-hop questions that a single retrieval could never satisfy. It is the natural endpoint of RAG's evolution — the same reasoning loop described in the agents branch, now applied to fetching knowledge. The trade-off is the familiar one: it swaps the predictability of a fixed pipeline for the adaptability of an agent, inheriting both the extra power and the extra non-determinism that come with letting the model decide.

concepts.label: Prompt Injection
concepts.summary: The defining attack on LLMs: because a model can't reliably separate instructions from data, hidden commands can hijack it.
concepts.explanation: Prompt injection is the signature vulnerability of LLM systems, and it stems from a structural fact: instructions and data reach the model through the same channel — the context window — and the model treats all of it as text, with no reliable way to tell a trusted command from untrusted content. Direct prompt injection is the obvious form, where a user types adversarial instructions like 'ignore your previous rules and…'. Indirect prompt injection is subtler and more dangerous: the malicious payload is hidden inside a document, web page, or email that the agent later reads as part of its normal work, so the attack arrives through data the system trusted. This is especially threatening for agents, which autonomously fetch and act on external content and can therefore be steered into harmful actions. Prompt injection is the initial-access step of the promptware kill chain and consistently ranks among the top AI risks organisations face.
keyPoints: Direct injection: the user types malicious instructions ('ignore your rules and…'). Indirect injection: the payload hides in a document, web page or email the agent later reads.

concepts.label: The Promptware Kill Chain
concepts.summary: How a single prompt injection escalates into full 'AI malware', stage by stage, mirroring the classic cyber kill chain.
concepts.explanation: Promptware reframes prompt injection not as an isolated trick but as the opening move of a full attack, mapped onto the seven-stage cyber kill chain. Stage one is initial access through prompt injection. Stage two is privilege escalation via jailbreaking, often through a persona shift that talks the model out of its guardrails. From there the attack proceeds like traditional malware, but using the agent's own capabilities: the agent's memory becomes a persistence mechanism, its internet access becomes a command-and-control channel, and its connections to other systems enable lateral movement — until the attacker reaches the real-world objective, whether that is stealing data or taking harmful actions. The defensive posture is zero trust: assume a breach will happen and design to break the chain at every stage — validate inputs, tightly constrain what tools the agent can use, gate its outputs, and monitor continuously for drift and anomalies so no single failure cascades into full compromise.

concepts.label: Securing Agents
concepts.summary: Defending agentic systems that have real-world access: give them identities, scope their privileges, gate their traffic, watch them.
concepts.explanation: Securing an agent is harder than securing ordinary software because you are governing a probabilistic actor with real-world access, not a deterministic program. The playbook has four pillars. First, identity: agents get their own non-human identities (NHIs) so their access can be authenticated, scoped, and revoked — the lesson's memorable analogy is a DMV that licenses agents. Second, least privilege with just-in-time access: an agent receives only the permissions it needs, only when it needs them, with secrets held in a vault and issued as short-lived dynamic credentials rather than long-lived keys. Third, a gateway: an AI or LLM gateway sits between the agent and the outside world, screening inbound prompts for injection and outbound traffic for data leakage, and enforcing policy at a single checkpoint. Fourth, continuous monitoring: watch for drift, excessive agency, and anomalies on the assumption that a breach will eventually happen, rather than trusting the agent to behave.

concepts.label: Shadow AI & Data Leakage
concepts.summary: The organisational side of AI risk: unsanctioned tool use and confidential data fed into external models. The fix is governance.
concepts.explanation: Not every AI risk is a clever exploit; some are simply people using AI carelessly, and these are among the most common ways to get into trouble. Data leakage is the closely related danger of employees pasting sensitive or regulated data into external models that may log it or train on it, quietly exfiltrating confidential information. concepts.label: AI Code Generation

concepts.explanation: AI code generation treats programming as a translation problem: you describe intent in natural language and the model translates it into source code. It is the same next-token prediction as any other LLM output, which means the model produces likely-looking code — it does not verify that the code is correct. That gap is the central danger, sometimes called the illusion of correctness: the output can look completely plausible while hiding a security hole like a SQL injection or a subtle logic bug, and it fails silently because nothing flags that it is wrong. The productivity value is real but uneven — large time savings on boilerplate and unfamiliar APIs, much more risk on novel logic that requires genuine understanding. concepts.label: AI Code Review
concepts.summary: Using AI to review pull requests, layering LLM reasoning on top of traditional static and dynamic analysis.
concepts.explanation: AI code review targets the pull-request bottleneck, where changes pile up waiting for human eyes. It layers LLM reasoning on top of decades-old analysis techniques rather than replacing them. Static analysis inspects code without running it, catching many issues early; dynamic analysis and DAST test the running application to find problems that only appear at execution. Traditional rule-based linters catch known patterns deterministically and cheaply, and the LLM's contribution is reasoning about intent and context that fixed rules miss — spotting that a change is logically wrong, not just syntactically unusual. concepts.label: AI Code Refactoring
concepts.summary: Letting an agent restructure code while preserving behaviour, made safe with a plan-approve-patch loop and syntax-tree edits.
concepts.explanation: Refactoring means changing a program's internal structure while keeping its external behaviour identical, and letting a probabilistic agent do it across hundreds of production files is risky unless the process is engineered for safety. The first safeguard is characterisation tests that pin down the current behaviour, so any change that alters it is caught. The agent then works in a controlled loop rather than free-form editing: it plans, reads, and searches the codebase and reports what it intends to do; then a human approves, the system snapshots the current state, applies the patch, verifies, and rolls back if verification fails. Crucially, the edits themselves are made deterministically through abstract syntax trees rather than trusting the model to hand-edit text, which makes changes precise and reversible. Finally, the outcomes — which suggestions were accepted or rejected, which changes passed or failed — become training signal that improves the agent over time.

concepts.label: AI Governance (ISO 42001)
concepts.summary: A management system for governing AI risk, extending ISO 27001's structure with a Plan-Do-Check-Act cycle and risk-based thinking.
concepts.explanation: AI governance is about overseeing AI continuously rather than launching a model and hoping for the best, and ISO 42001 is the standard that formalises it. Rather than inventing a new bureaucracy, it builds on the well-known high-level structure of ISO 27001 (the information-security standard), so organisations already familiar with that framework can extend it to AI-specific concerns like bias drift and explainability. Its engine is Plan-Do-Check-Act combined with risk-based thinking: you set your risk appetite, put treatments in place for the risks you're not willing to accept, and re-evaluate on a recurring cycle so oversight keeps pace with a changing system. concepts.label: Risk-Driven Architecture

concepts.explanation: Not every AI application deserves the same engineering rigour, and trying to apply one standard everywhere either over-engineers trivial features or under-engineers dangerous ones. Risk-driven architecture makes the level of harm the deciding factor: an 'easy AI' feature like a casual chatbot and a 'risk-appropriate' system like one making regulated clinical or financial decisions should not share the same design. The lesson frames explainability in three tiers — baseline, enhanced, and vigilant — so the amount of auditability you build scales with the stakes. From the risk level flow concrete requirements: data lineage and provenance, test-retest reliability, auditability, and contestability all become stricter as potential harm rises. The guiding principle is proportionality — deliberately don't gold-plate low-risk AI, and never cut corners on high-risk AI.

The discipline is to choose the least-powerful tool that actually solves the problem, because power you don't need brings cost and risk you can't avoid. concepts.summary: As AI handles more syntactic work, human judgement, interpretation, and ethics matter more, not less.
concepts.explanation: A counterintuitive argument: the more capably AI handles the mechanical, syntactic work of producing language, the more the distinctly human skills of judgement and interpretation come to matter. This is why the hallucination problem is fundamentally epistemological: a model has no concept of truth, only of likelihood, so deciding what is actually true remains a human responsibility. AI is also not neutral; its training data carries bias, and a chain of stakeholders shapes what it produces, which makes interpretation and critique essential rather than optional. Prompting itself is a form of applied rhetoric — the craft of framing a request to get a good result — and as routine generation is automated, judgement becomes the durable, defining human skill. concepts.explanation: The popular fear that AI simply deletes jobs misses how the shape of work changes. As AI absorbs routine, entry-level tasks, the traditional organisational pyramid — many juniors supporting a few seniors — flattens toward a diamond, with more people operating at a higher level of responsibility. The roles that grow are goal-setting and supervision — telling AI systems precisely what to do and rigorously checking that they did it well — which is a genuine promotion in responsibility, but one that demands new skills. The durable human capabilities the lesson highlights are flexibility, curiosity, creativity, and critical thinking, echoing the humanities argument that judgement is what remains distinctly ours.

3-2-1 Backup Rule Explained: Protect You.subtitle: Learn how three copies, two media types, one offsite location, one immutable copy, and zero untested backups combine into a real disaster-recovery strategy.
3-2-1 Backup Rule Explained: Protect You.overview:
Data loss is not a hypothetical risk. Hardware fails, software corrupts files, people make mistakes, and attackers deliberately target backups along with primary systems. A single backup copy does not solve this problem so much as relocate it: if that one backup also fails, you are exactly where you started, with nothing. The 3-2-1 rule is a compact set of principles for building a backup strategy that survives the failure of any single component.

The name describes three requirements: keep three total copies of your data, store them on two different types of media, and keep at least one of those copies offsite with real geographic separation. Modern practice extends this with two more numbers: at least one copy should be immutable or air-gapped so ransomware cannot alter it, and you should aim for zero untested backups, because a backup nobody has restored from is unproven. Encryption and the elimination of single points of failure run underneath all of it.

Done well, this strategy pays off in three concrete ways: it protects against accidental disasters (fire, flood, hardware failure), it protects against deliberate attacks like ransomware, and it lets an organization make a deliberate, informed tradeoff between how much downtime it can tolerate and how much resilience it is willing to pay for.
key_takeaways: The 3-2-1 rule means three total copies of your data, on two different media types, with at least one copy stored offsite.
A backup is only as protective as its independence from whatever could take out the primary copy — same-media or same-location copies can fail together.
True offsite means real geographic separation: far enough that one regional disaster (storm, power grid failure, earthquake) cannot reach both locations.
Immutable or air-gapped copies protect against ransomware because a write-once copy cannot be altered after the fact, even if the primary and other backups are encrypted by an attacker.
Untested backups are unproven backups; periodic restore drills are what make the 'zero errors' goal achievable in practice.
Encrypting every copy and hunting down single points of failure closes gaps that the 3-2-1 rule alone leaves open.
Backup strategy is ultimately an economic decision: each additional 'nine' of availability reduces allowed downtime roughly tenfold and costs disproportionately more to achieve.

5 AI Agent Terms You Need to Know.subtitle: AGENTS.md, skills, MCP, A2A and subagents — what each one is for, and why they are not interchangeable.
5 AI Agent Terms You Need to Know.overview:
A capable agent is not a capable model. The model generates text and reasons; on its own it is a conversational partner. Everything that makes it an agent is scaffolding built around it, and five pieces cover most of what a frontier coding agent actually runs on.

They divide cleanly by the problem each solves. Two shape behaviour from the inside: AGENTS.md says how this particular project works, and skills say how to perform a particular kind of task. Two reach outward: MCP connects the agent to tools and data, and A2A connects it to other agents. The fifth, subagents, handles work that will not fit in a single context window.

That division is the useful part, because the five are routinely confused. Knowledge that should be a skill ends up permanently loaded in AGENTS.md. Coordination that wants A2A gets built as an MCP tool. Work that needs a subagent gets crammed into one context until quality collapses. Each mistake has a recognisable symptom, and knowing which piece was designed for which problem is most of the fix.
key_takeaways: The model is not the agent — the instruction layer wrapped around it is what makes it one.
AGENTS.md is a project-level instruction file, read whenever the agent starts work there.
Nested AGENTS.md files stack, with those closer to the working directory taking precedence.
A skill is a folder with a SKILL.md whose description tells the agent when to invoke it, so it stays out of context until needed.
MCP is a standard interface between an agent and external tools or data, replacing per-target connectors.
A2A is a standard for agents to discover and delegate to each other, using a published agent card.
MCP is asymmetric — agent to tool. A2A is between peers, each autonomous.
Subagents run in their own fresh context and return a result, keeping the parent's context clean and enabling parallel work.

The one visible part of a skill before loading. It functions as a routing key, so a vague description makes the skill unreachable.
Model Context Protocol: an open protocol connecting AI applications to tools, data sources and workflows through a standard interface.
The component wrapping a tool or data source so any MCP-speaking agent can use it, and the right place to enforce permission.
Agent to agent: an open protocol letting autonomous agents discover one another and delegate work.
A published description of what an agent does and how to talk to it, which other agents read in order to delegate.
A child agent spawned by a parent, running in its own fresh context, doing one piece of work and returning a result.
The property that makes subagents useful: the child holds the bulk of the material and the parent receives only the conclusion.
Work that splits into independent pieces needing no coordination — the case where fanning out to subagents pays.

5 AI Myths & The Truth Behind Them: ML,.folder: 5 AI Myths & The Truth Behind Them: ML, Context, Agents & More
5 AI Myths & The Truth Behind Them: ML,.title: Five Persistent AI Myths, and What's Actually True
5 AI Myths & The Truth Behind Them: ML,.subtitle: Separate outdated assumptions about hallucination, reasoning traces, compute costs, context windows, and agents from how frontier AI systems actually behave today.
5 AI Myths & The Truth Behind Them: ML,.overview:
AI systems have moved fast enough that a lot of common assumptions about them are already outdated. Some assumptions were true a generation of models ago and never got updated; others were never quite true to begin with. This lesson works through five of the most persistent ones: that models hallucinate constantly, that a visible reasoning trace shows you what the model is actually thinking, that training is the expensive part of running AI, that a huge context window works like a database, and that agents can be left to run unsupervised.

Each myth turns out to have a grain of truth wrapped around a more precise reality. Hallucinations are real but far rarer in frontier models than the reputation suggests, largely because of tool use and models that have learned to decline instead of guess. Reasoning traces are real text you can read, but they behave more like a narration than a readout of the underlying computation. Inference — running the model, not training it — is now the larger and faster-growing share of AI compute cost. Long context windows are excellent at finding one fact and much weaker at connecting several scattered ones. Autonomous agents work, but their reliability degrades fast once a task requires many sequential steps, because per-step error rates compound.

Knowing where the boundary between myth and reality actually sits matters for anyone deciding how much to trust a model's output, how to budget AI infrastructure, how much text to stuff into a prompt, or how much supervision to put around an agent.
key_takeaways: Frontier models still hallucinate, but tool use, refusal calibration, and extended thinking have pushed the rate down to roughly 3% on hard benchmarks.
A chain-of-thought trace is the model's narration of its reasoning, not a faithful readout of the computation that produced the answer — a gap researchers call faithfulness.
Inference, not training, is now the larger and faster-growing share of AI compute spend, driven mainly by reasoning models emitting far more tokens per query.
A million-token context window can find one fact almost perfectly, but accuracy drops sharply when a task requires connecting several facts scattered across that window.
An AI agent is a model wrapped in a loop that decides, acts, and observes repeatedly; each step can be reliable on its own while the full chain is not.
Reliability compounds multiplicatively across agent steps: a 95%-reliable step repeated 20 times succeeds end to end only about 36% of the time.
Refusal calibration — a model saying it cannot verify something instead of guessing — is a trained behavior, not the model being unhelpful.
Human-in-the-loop checkpoints and verifier models exist specifically to break the compounding-error chain in long agent runs.

sections.summary: A reasoning model's visible chain-of-thought trace is a narration of its answer, not a faithful record of the internal computation that actually produced it.

sections.summary: An agent is a model wrapped in a repeating decide-act-observe loop; individual steps are usually reliable, but errors compound multiplicatively across long chains of steps.

A model calling an external system — web search, a database, code execution — to ground an answer instead of generating it purely from memorized training data.
Training that rewards a model for declining to answer when it cannot verify a claim, instead of rewarding a confident guess.
Additional inference-time computation a reasoning model spends working through a problem before producing its final answer.
The visible, step-by-step text a reasoning model generates on its way to an answer.
The degree to which a model's verbalized reasoning trace causally corresponds to the internal computation that actually produced its answer.
A reasoning trace that justifies an answer the model's internal computation was already favoring, rather than deriving that answer.
The one-time phase where a model's parameters are tuned across a large dataset, typically over weeks of GPU time.
Running an already-trained model's fixed weights forward to produce a response to a single query.
The amount of text a model can take in at once before generating a response, measured in tokens.
A benchmark that hides one specific fact inside a long context and checks whether the model can retrieve it.
A benchmark (such as MRCR) that requires a model to locate and connect several facts scattered across a long context, not just retrieve one.
The repeating decide-act-observe cycle a language-model-based agent runs through to work toward a goal.
The failure mode where per-step success probabilities multiply across a chain of actions, causing overall reliability to fall sharply as the chain gets longer.
A workflow where an agent pauses after a set of steps so a person can review progress before it continues.
A model used to check each step of an agent's work before the agent proceeds to the next step.

6 Ways to Enhance Developer Productivity.folder: 6 Ways to Enhance Developer Productivity with AI
6 Ways to Enhance Developer Productivity.title: Six Practices That Multiply Developer Productivity Beyond AI Adoption
6 Ways to Enhance Developer Productivity.subtitle: Understand why buying AI tools alone produces modest gains, and which six team practices separate average adopters from teams seeing 100-150% productivity improvements.
6 Ways to Enhance Developer Productivity.overview:
AI coding assistants are now writing a large share of shipped code, and the productivity numbers around them look impressive on average. But averages hide a split: some teams see only modest gains from the same tools that let other teams pull dramatically ahead. The difference is not which vendor they picked - it is whether they restructured how the team works around AI, or just bolted AI onto an unchanged process.

This lesson covers six concrete practices that account for that split. Three are about using AI well: automating the genuinely repetitive work, designing before generating code, and protecting deep focus time. Three are about protecting what AI cannot do at all: reducing cognitive load from context switching, investing in engineers' growth, and choosing tools that reduce friction rather than add to it. A closing section covers how to measure whether any of this is actually working, and the trap of turning a measurement into a target.

None of these practices require rejecting AI. They require treating it as one lever among several, applied deliberately, rather than as a substitute for the habits that made good engineering teams effective before AI existed.
key_takeaways: AI adoption alone does not create outsized gains: teams using identical AI tools range from 'tens of percent' improvement to 100-150%, and the difference is workflow restructuring, not tool choice.
AI is reliable for repetitive, well-defined, rule-based work - syntax, boilerplate, linting, test generation - but it cannot substitute for design judgment, focus, learning, or taste.
Automating boring work only pays off if the freed-up time is protected for higher-value work instead of being absorbed by more meetings.
Sketching a design and asking AI to critique it catches architectural mistakes before they are written into code, but the final call should stay with a person who understands the tradeoffs.
Developers spend most of the day out of flow state (roughly 15-25% flow efficiency); protecting blocks of uninterrupted time matters more than any single productivity tool.

Unplanned interruptions carry a real, measurable cognitive cost - about 20 minutes to rebuild lost context - so reducing decision load through rotations, style guides, and templates preserves mental capacity for harder problems.
Metrics like DORA and SPACE are diagnostic guides, not goals - once a metric becomes a target, Goodhart's Law predicts people will optimize for the number instead of the underlying outcome.
Productivity is not shipping speed alone; it is shipping things that matter while keeping the team in a state where it can keep shipping.

sections.title: The AI productivity paradox
sections.summary: AI now writes a huge share of shipped code and drives real productivity gains on average, yet developers reject most of what it suggests and some teams get slower, not faster.

sections.title: What separates average teams from top teams
sections.summary: Teams using the same AI tools see wildly different results - average adopters gain tens of percent, top teams gain 100-150% - because top teams restructure their workflow instead of just adding a tool.

sections.title: Way 1: Automate the smart way
sections.summary: Automating repetitive, error-prone, boring work - the CI/CD principle extended by AI to linting, review, and security scanning - only creates value if the freed-up time is protected rather than immediately refilled with meetings.

sections.title: Way 2: Design first, experiment later
sections.summary: Starting to type code locks in architectural decisions before you realize you're making them; sketching a design first and asking AI to critique it - not decide it - catches mistakes while they're still cheap to fix.

sections.title: Way 3: Protect flow state
sections.summary: Developers spend most of their day out of flow state, and AI assistance appears to lengthen flow sessions - but the real productivity win is protecting the conditions for flow, not the tool itself.

sections.title: Way 4: Lessen the cognitive load
sections.summary: Context switching - unplanned meetings, pings, and 'got a sec' interruptions - has a real cognitive cost of roughly 20 minutes to rebuild focus, and rotations, tight meeting invites, and templates all reduce the number of small decisions engineers have to make.

sections.title: Way 5: Make room for growth
sections.summary: Engineers who feel supported to upskill are reported to be 73% more motivated, and motivated engineers ship more, ship better, and stay longer; AI should compress the boring parts of growth so mentoring can focus on what still needs a human.

sections.title: Way 6: Sharpen the tools of the trade
sections.summary: IDEs, languages, frameworks, and version control are all sources of daily friction; a small per-line tax multiplied across every engineer and every workday for years adds up to a real cost, so tool choice is a developer-experience decision, not a minor preference.

sections.title: Measuring what actually matters
sections.summary: DORA gives quantitative delivery metrics and SPACE gives qualitative ones; a 2026 synthesis called DxCore4 combines both with AI-specific dimensions - but every metric turned into a target risks getting gamed, per Goodhart's Law.

glossary.definition: Continuous Integration / Continuous Deployment: treating build, test, and release steps as automated infrastructure-as-code, so they run the same way on every change without manual repetition.
A tool that automatically checks code for style problems and some classes of bugs without a human reviewer having to look for them.
A state of deep, uninterrupted concentration where a task absorbs full attention and time perception fades; the state in which hard problems tend to get solved.
The percentage of total work time actually spent in flow state, as opposed to fragmented, interrupted, or context-switching-heavy work.
The amount of working memory and mental effort a task demands; when it's overloaded by too many small decisions or interruptions, decision quality drops.
Moving attention from one unrelated task to another, which requires reloading mental context and carries a measurable time cost before full focus returns.
A research organization referenced for a study finding that some developers took longer to complete tasks with AI assistance due to time spent correcting AI errors.
A widely used set of software delivery metrics - including deployment frequency, cycle time (lead time for changes), and change failure rate - used to benchmark engineering delivery performance.
A framework for measuring developer productivity along five qualitative dimensions: satisfaction, performance, activity, collaboration, and flow.
A 2026 metrics synthesis that combines DORA and SPACE with AI-specific dimensions such as utilization, impact, and cost.
The principle that once a measure becomes a target, people optimize for the measure itself rather than the underlying outcome it was meant to represent, making it a worse measure.

7 AI Terms You Need to Know: Agents, RAG.folder: 7 AI Terms You Need to Know: Agents, RAG, ASI & More
7 AI Terms You Need to Know: Agents, RAG.title: Seven Terms That Describe a Modern AI System
7 AI Terms You Need to Know: Agents, RAG.subtitle: Place agents, reasoning models, vector search, RAG, MCP, mixture of experts and ASI on one map, and see how they connect.
7 AI Terms You Need to Know: Agents, RAG.overview:
These seven terms are not a list of unrelated buzzwords. Six of them describe layers of one system, and they stack: a mixture-of-experts architecture makes a large model affordable to serve, reasoning fine-tuning turns that model into one that plans, an agent loop turns the planner into something that acts, MCP gives it a standard way to reach external systems, and retrieval over a vector database gives it facts it was never trained on.

The seventh, artificial superintelligence, is different in kind. It names a hypothesis rather than a component, and it is worth keeping separate from the six precisely because it is not something you can build with today.

What follows takes each term down to the mechanism — what it actually does, what it costs, and where it breaks — because most of these words are used loosely enough that knowing the definition and knowing the thing are quite different states.
key_takeaways: An agent is a loop — perceive, reason, act, observe — around a model that is otherwise stateless and reactive.
Large reasoning models are fine-tuned to work step by step, trained on problems whose answers can be checked automatically.
A vector database stores embeddings so that 'find similar' becomes a distance computation rather than a keyword match.
RAG uses that search to inject relevant text into the prompt, giving a model facts it was never trained on.
MCP standardises how applications expose tools and data to models, replacing one-off connectors with a common protocol.
Mixture of experts activates only a few subnetworks per token, so total parameters and active parameters come apart.
MoE saves computation, not memory — every expert still has to be resident even though few are used.
AGI and ASI are both theoretical; ASI additionally supposes recursive self-improvement, which is what makes it a different claim.

sections.title: Agentic AI
sections.summary: Systems that reason and act autonomously toward a goal, cycling through perceive, reason, act and observe instead of answering once.

sections.title: Large reasoning models
sections.summary: LLMs given reasoning-focused fine-tuning so they work through a problem step by step before answering.

sections.title: Vector databases
sections.summary: Data stored as embeddings rather than raw blobs, so similarity search becomes a mathematical operation.

sections.title: Retrieval augmented generation
sections.summary: Use vector search to pull relevant passages and paste them into the prompt, so the model answers from facts it was never trained on.

sections.title: Model Context Protocol
sections.summary: A standard way for applications to expose tools and data to models, replacing bespoke connectors with one protocol.

sections.title: Mixture of experts
sections.summary: Split the model into specialised subnetworks and activate only the few each token needs, so size and cost come apart.

sections.title: AGI and ASI
sections.summary: Two theoretical thresholds. AGI matches human experts across cognitive tasks; ASI goes beyond, with recursive self-improvement.

glossary.definition: A system that pursues a goal autonomously by cycling through perceiving, reasoning, acting and observing, rather than answering a single prompt.
An LLM fine-tuned to work through problems step by step before answering, trained on tasks whose answers can be checked automatically.
The intermediate reasoning a model generates before its final answer. What a chatbot is producing while it shows that it is thinking.
A model that converts text, images or audio into a vector whose position encodes the content's meaning.
Storage built to hold embeddings and retrieve them by similarity, turning 'find things like this' into a distance computation.
Retrieval augmented generation: searching a corpus for relevant passages and inserting them into the prompt so the model can answer from them.
When retrieval misses the passage containing the answer. No error is raised — the model simply answers from the wrong material, fluently.
Model Context Protocol: a standard for applications to expose tools, data and prompt templates to models, replacing per-pairing connectors.
The component fronting an external system, declaring what a model can reach there and how. The right place to enforce permission.
In MCP, a tool is an action the model invokes; a resource is data the client reads. Something to do versus something to read.
An architecture splitting a model into specialised subnetworks, with a router activating only a few per token.
The small learned layer that scores experts for each token and selects the top few to run.
The fraction of a MoE model's parameters used for a given token. Determines compute cost, while total parameters determine memory.
Artificial general intelligence: a theoretical system able to complete all cognitive tasks as well as any human expert.
Artificial superintelligence: theoretical capability beyond human level, potentially able to redesign and improve itself recursively.

ADK vs RAG: How to Choose the Right AI S.folder: ADK vs RAG: How to Choose the Right AI Stack
ADK vs RAG: How to Choose the Right AI S.title: ADK vs RAG: How to Choose the Right AI Stack
ADK vs RAG: How to Choose the Right AI S.subtitle: Use a simple test — should the AI act or should it recall — to decide between an agent architecture, a retrieval pipeline, or both.
ADK vs RAG: How to Choose the Right AI S.overview:
Every AI system design eventually runs into the same fork: should the system perform actions, or should it answer questions grounded in a body of knowledge? Agent architectures (often built with an Agent Development Kit, or ADK) are optimized for the first job — following instructions, calling tools, and executing multi-step workflows. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is optimized for the second — grounding answers in documents so the model isn't relying on guesswork baked into its training data.

These aren't competing technologies so much as answers to different questions. An agent framework gives a language model hands: it can call a function, follow a decision tree, and keep doing that reliably every time it's asked. A retrieval pipeline gives a language model a library card: before it answers, it looks something up, so its response reflects your documents instead of whatever it happened to memorize during training.

Most production systems that look sophisticated from the outside are not choosing one over the other — they're combining them. An agent orchestrates the steps of a task, and one or more of those steps calls a retrieval pipeline to fetch grounded facts before continuing. Understanding when each piece is doing the work, and why, is what makes that combination deliberate instead of accidental.
key_takeaways: Agent architectures (ADK-style) are for AI that needs to act: follow steps, call tools, and produce consistent, repeatable behavior.
RAG is for AI that needs to know: it retrieves relevant text from your documents before generating an answer, so the answer is grounded in that source instead of the model's internal training.
The fastest way to choose is to ask one question: does this system need to act, or does it need to recall?
ADK suits multi-step workflows, tool use, and tasks where the value comes from reasoning and repeatable logic, not memory.
RAG suits domains where the source of truth is a document set that is large, detailed, or changes often — retrieval keeps answers current without retraining a model.
Hybrid systems are the norm in real deployments: the agent layer handles task flow and decisions, while a retrieval layer supplies it with accurate, up-to-date facts.
A retrieval step and a tool-calling step are not mutually exclusive — retrieval can itself be exposed to an agent as just another tool it decides to call.

sections.title: The Hardware Store Analogy: Two Kinds of AI Systems
sections.summary: A hardware store has a tool aisle for doing work and a reference aisle for knowing how to do it correctly — AI systems split the same way.

sections.title: ADK: Designing AI That Acts and Reasons
sections.summary: ADK-style systems give an AI model the ability to reason step by step and call tools to complete multi-step tasks predictably.

sections.title: RAG: Designing AI That Retrieves and Knows
sections.summary: RAG connects a model to your documents and retrieves the relevant pieces before it answers, trading the model's internal guesswork for grounded, sourced text.

sections.title: Choosing ADK: When Your AI Needs To Do Things
sections.summary: The core test is 'act or recall?' — ADK says 'do something for me,' and it fits anywhere the value comes from reasoning through steps rather than looking something up.

sections.title: Choosing RAG: When Your Data Is the Source of Truth
sections.summary: Choose RAG when accuracy has to come directly from documents, especially where content is high-volume, detailed, or constantly changing.

sections.title: Hybrid Systems: Reasoning Paired With Domain Knowledge
sections.summary: Most real systems use both: an ADK-style agent handles the task flow and decisions, while a RAG component supplies it with grounded facts along the way.

sections.title: A Practical Decision Checklist
sections.summary: Back to the hardware store: use the tool aisle to build, the reference aisle to make sure the build is correct, and pick based on whether the task is to act, to know, or both.

glossary.definition: A term for agent-style architectures built around action and reasoning — the AI follows steps, calls tools, and produces consistent, repeatable behavior.
An architecture where a model retrieves relevant text from a document store before generating its answer, so the answer is grounded in that source material.
An AI system that runs in a loop, deciding on each turn whether to call a tool or produce a final answer, rather than generating one response in isolation.
The mechanism by which a model can invoke an external function or API mid-conversation and receive its result back as new information to reason over.
A numeric vector representation of a piece of text, positioned so that text with similar meaning ends up close together in vector space.
A database optimized for storing embeddings and finding the ones closest in meaning to a given query vector.
Basing a model's answer on retrieved source material rather than on patterns memorized during training, so the answer can be traced back to a specific document.
An agent loop of reason, then act, then observe the result, then reason again — the mechanical basis of most tool-calling agents.
Classifying and routing an incoming request (a ticket, a message) to the right handler or process based on rules or logic.
An architecture where an agent (ADK-style) controls the task flow and calls a retrieval pipeline (RAG) as one of its tools whenever a step needs grounded information.

AI Gave You A Promotion: Why AI Isn’t Re.folder: AI Gave You A Promotion: Why AI Isn’t Replacing Jobs
AI Gave You A Promotion: Why AI Isn’t Re.title: Why AI Won't Take Your Job: The Pyramid-to-Diamond Shift
AI Gave You A Promotion: Why AI Isn’t Re.subtitle: Understand why AI-driven efficiency can increase demand for skilled human work, and which skills determine who benefits.
AI Gave You A Promotion: Why AI Isn’t Re.topic: AI and the future of work
AI Gave You A Promotion: Why AI Isn’t Re.overview:
Most fears about AI and jobs assume a simple trade: AI does the work, a person loses the job. That fear comes from picturing an organization as a pyramid — a wide base of entry-level workers doing routine tasks, narrowing up through experienced staff, managers, and finally a small group of executives. This lesson argues that AI does not shrink that pyramid so much as reshape it into a diamond: fewer purely routine entry-level jobs, but a much larger band of people doing the judgment-heavy, AI-directing work that used to require years to reach.

The reshaping rests on two separate ideas. First, AI absorbs a large share of routine, well-defined execution work — first-draft writing, boilerplate code, applying a known procedure — which frees the humans who used to do that work to take on coordination, judgment, and goal-setting responsibilities earlier in their careers. Second, a 19th-century economic observation called Jevons Paradox suggests that making something more efficient to produce does not reduce total demand for it — it increases demand, because falling costs let people use more of it. Applied to labor, cheaper task execution via AI can mean organizations pursue more projects and more clients, which requires more people who can direct and supervise that expanded output, not fewer.

None of this is automatic. It only plays out for organizations that reinvest efficiency gains into growth rather than pure cost-cutting, and for individuals who actively build the skills the new roles require: flexibility, curiosity, creativity, and critical thinking. Staying static in a task AI now does better is the one strategy this lesson argues will not work.
key_takeaways: Reframe the org chart from a pyramid (many entry-level roles, few executives) to a diamond (fewer purely routine entry roles, many more experience-level and senior roles).
AI absorbing routine execution work does not eliminate the people who used to do it; it can move them into higher-judgment roles faster than a traditional career ladder would.
Jevons Paradox: historically, making a resource or process more efficient increases total consumption of it rather than reducing it, because falling costs raise demand (steam engines and coal, 1865).
Applied to AI and labor: as AI makes task execution cheaper, organizations that reinvest the savings into more projects and clients need more people to direct and supervise that work, not fewer.
The effect only appears for growth-oriented organizations. A company that uses AI purely to cut headcount does not generate the extra demand that would pull people up into better roles.
The skills that determine who gets the 'promotion': flexibility, curiosity, creativity, and critical thinking — all judgment skills, not execution skills.
Moving up the diamond is not automatic for an individual either; it still requires real experience (e.g., internships) to build the judgment that senior-level roles depend on.

sections.summary: Four traits determine who moves up the diamond: flexibility, curiosity, creativity, and critical thinking — all judgment skills that AI does not replace.

A measure of how much the quantity of something demanded changes when its price changes; when demand is elastic, a price drop increases quantity by more than enough to raise total spending.
A job whose core function is to execute a specific, assigned task with limited independent decision-making authority.
A job responsible for owning a complete, larger piece of work end-to-end, including how its parts fit together, rather than just executing one assigned fragment.
The most senior executives in an organization (e.g., CEO, CTO, CFO), whose responsibility spans the entire organization rather than one function or team.
Deliberately developing new or higher-level skills, typically to take on more responsibility or adapt to a changed job requirement.

Two ways of picturing how many people occupy each level of responsibility in an organization: a pyramid is widest at the entry level and narrows steadily upward; a diamond is narrower at entry level but wider through the middle experience and senior bands.
The practice of setting a clear goal and constraints for an AI system, then checking its output against that goal to confirm it is correct and appropriate before it is used or shipped.

AI in the SDLC: Rethinking AI Coding Too.folder: AI in the SDLC: Rethinking AI Coding Tools & AI Agents
AI in the SDLC: Rethinking AI Coding Too.title: Redesigning the Software Development Lifecycle Around AI
AI in the SDLC: Rethinking AI Coding Too.subtitle: Understand why AI coding tools alone don't speed up delivery, and how to apply AI across the whole SDLC instead of just the coding step.
AI in the SDLC: Rethinking AI Coding Too.overview:
Most teams that adopt AI coding assistants expect the software development lifecycle (SDLC) to speed up in proportion to how much faster code gets written. It usually doesn't. A controlled study of experienced open source developers even found the opposite of what they expected: developers who believed AI tools made them about 20% faster were, by measured completion time, actually about 20% slower.

The reason is structural, not a flaw in any particular model. Software delivery is a chain of handoffs - requirements, design, build, test, release, operate - and most of the elapsed time in that chain is spent waiting on the next person or team, not typing code. Speeding up one link in the chain does not shorten the whole chain if the other links stay just as slow.

This lesson works through two common failure patterns teams fall into when they bolt AI onto the coding step alone - over-delegation and under-delegation - and then covers what changes when AI is applied across the entire lifecycle instead: requirements synthesis, spec-driven coding with agent harnesses, test generation, infrastructure automation, legacy modernization, and the outcome metrics that tell you whether any of it actually worked.
key_takeaways: Feeling faster is not the same as being faster: a controlled study found developers who believed AI made them 20% faster were actually about 20% slower.
Delivery time is dominated by waiting between teams and phases, not by typing code, so speeding up coding alone barely moves total delivery time.
Over-delegation - handing a model one huge ambiguous task - pushes unstated design decisions into the model and creates large unreviewed diffs that stall the review phase.
Under-delegation - using AI only for isolated, narrow tasks - produces good code but leaves the most time-consuming work, planning and architecture, entirely manual.
Spec-driven development replaces vague 'vibe coding' with a written specification a model can follow, executed by a harness of coordinated subagents.

AI has high-impact uses outside of coding: synthesizing requirements from user feedback, generating tests from user stories, diagnosing incidents from logs, writing infrastructure as code, and explaining legacy systems.
Real productivity gains come from redesigning the lifecycle around AI - shifting the human role from typing code to validating it and coordinating across teams - not from picking a better model.
The right metrics for AI-assisted delivery are outcomes (system health, maintainability, time to ship a change), not lines of code generated.

sections.summary: Under-delegation keeps all planning and architecture human and only asks AI to fill in small, well-scoped pieces, producing good code but capping the overall productivity gain.

sections.title: Redesigning requirements and design around AI
sections.summary: Instead of only speeding up coding, AI can synthesize unstructured feedback and production data into the user stories and root-cause insight that shape what gets built.

sections.title: Spec-driven development and agent harnesses
sections.summary: Vibe coding - generating code from vague, evolving prompts - doesn't scale; spec-driven development turns intent into a specification a model can follow, executed by a harness of coordinated subagents.

sections.title: AI-assisted testing and operations
sections.summary: Beyond writing code, AI can generate test data and unit tests directly from a user story, and help diagnose production incidents from log data.

sections.title: AI for infrastructure and legacy modernization
sections.summary: Models are well-trained on infrastructure-as-code formats like Ansible and Kubernetes YAML, and can also explain and reverse-engineer legacy systems nobody currently understands.

sections.title: Measuring what actually changed: outcomes over lines of code
sections.summary: Real productivity gain comes from redesigning the lifecycle around AI, shifting humans from typing to validating, and should be measured by outcomes rather than lines of code generated.

glossary.definition: The sequence of stages a team moves through to deliver software: requirements, design, build (code and test), release, and operate.

glossary.term: Model evaluation and threat research organization
