sections.title: What fine-tuning does to a model
sections.summary: Take a base model trained on a broad corpus and continue training it on a focused dataset, producing a new model with adjusted weights.

sections.title: The 2025 rematch
sections.summary: The same company built a legal benchmark and found seven general-purpose models, with no legal fine-tuning at all, had surpassed their custom one.

sections.title: Why general models caught up
sections.summary: Three changes: context windows grew enormously, reasoning moved to inference time, and inference got cheaper.

sections.title: Customisation without touching the weights
sections.summary: RAG supplies the knowledge, and context engineering assembles everything the model needs into a deliberately constructed prompt.

sections.title: Agent skills: packaging procedural knowledge
sections.summary: Folders of files that package how to do something and which tools to use, loaded on demand when the model meets a matching task.

sections.title: LoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
sections.summary: Train a small adapter over frozen base weights. Most of what is called fine-tuning in production today is some flavour of this.

sections.title: Where fine-tuning still wins
sections.summary: Three specific bottlenecks the no-weights stack cannot solve: hard latency limits, distillation into smaller models, and training against a programmatic grader.

sections.title: The decision order
sections.summary: Base model, then prompt and context engineering, then RAG, then skills — and fine-tuning only for a bottleneck the rest cannot clear.

glossary.definition: The off-the-shelf pre-trained model, from a frontier lab or open source, before any customisation.
Continuing a base model's training on a focused dataset so the domain behaviour ends up in the weights.
The problem that a fixed custom model competes against frontier models that keep improving, so its lead decays without anything changing.
How much text a model can process in one call. Growth from thousands to millions of tokens removed much of the need to bake knowledge into weights.
A model that performs extended step-by-step thinking at inference time, shifting capability from training to the moment of the question.
Deliberately assembling the prompt from parts — system role, retrieved data, examples, format rules — as a versioned, testable artefact.
A folder of files packaging procedural knowledge and the tools to apply it, loaded on demand by any capable model.
Low-rank adaptation: training two small matrices whose product approximates a weight update, while the base weights stay frozen.
Parameter-efficient fine-tuning: the family of methods, including LoRA, that adapt a model by training a small fraction of parameters.
The small trained artefact a PEFT method produces. Swappable, stackable against one base model, and removable.
The bottleneck width of a LoRA adapter, controlling its capacity and its parameter count.
Using a large teacher model to generate high-quality outputs, then fine-tuning a smaller student model on them.
Training against a grader rather than fixed answers: the model samples candidates, the grader scores them, and high scores are reinforced.
A programmatic scoring function used in RFT. Requires a definitive checkable answer, which is what limits where RFT applies.

Is RAG Still Needed? Choosing the Best A.folder: Is RAG Still Needed? Choosing the Best Approach for LLMs
Is RAG Still Needed? Choosing the Best A.title: RAG or Long Context: How to Get Data Into a Model
Is RAG Still Needed? Choosing the Best A.subtitle: Decide between retrieval and stuffing the context window using cost, recall and data size rather than fashion.
Is RAG Still Needed? Choosing the Best A.overview:
Language models are frozen in time. They know the world up to their training cutoff and nothing about what happened five minutes ago, nor anything about your internal wikis or proprietary codebase. Every application that needs current or private data therefore has to solve the same problem: get the right data into the model at the right time. This is context injection.

There are two answers. RAG is the engineering answer — chunk your documents, embed them, store the vectors, search at query time, inject the best matches. Long context is the brute-force answer — put the documents into the prompt and let the model's attention mechanism find what matters. For years the second was impossible because context windows were tiny. They are not tiny any more, which is why the question is live.

The honest answer is that the two fail in different places, and which failure you can afford decides the architecture. RAG can silently fail to retrieve the answer that was sitting right there. Long context makes you pay to re-read everything on every query, dilutes attention as it grows, and hits a hard ceiling long before enterprise data does. Neither is dead; they cover different regimes.
key_takeaways: Context injection is the shared problem: a frozen model needs current or private data supplied at query time.
RAG chunks and embeds documents ahead of time, then retrieves the closest matches per query and injects them.
Long context skips the retrieval stack entirely and lets the attention mechanism do the finding.
Long context collapses the infrastructure — no chunking strategy, no embedding model, no vector store, no reranker, no sync.
RAG's characteristic failure is silent: the answer existed in the data but retrieval never surfaced it, and nothing reports an error.
RAG cannot answer questions about what is absent, because it retrieves what exists and never sees the gap between two documents.
Long context re-pays the processing cost on every query; RAG pays it once at index time, and prompt caching only helps for static prefixes.
Attention dilutes as context grows, so more context is not monotonically better — and enterprise data will never fit regardless.

sections.title: The problem both approaches solve
sections.summary: Models are frozen at their training cutoff and have never seen your private data. Everything else follows from that.

sections.title: RAG: the engineering approach
sections.summary: Chunk the documents, embed them, store the vectors, search semantically at query time, inject the winners.

sections.title: Long context: the model-native approach
sections.summary: Skip the database and the embedding model. Put the documents in the prompt and let attention do the heavy lifting.

sections.title: What changed: three orders of magnitude
sections.summary: Early context windows held about 4K tokens. Today's frontier models handle a million and more, which is what makes the question worth asking.

sections.title: The case for long context: no stack, and no retrieval lottery
sections.summary: Two arguments. You delete most of the architecture, and you delete the failure mode that never announces itself.

sections.title: The whole-book problem: reasoning about what is absent
sections.summary: RAG retrieves what exists. Some questions are about what is missing, and no snippet contains a gap.

sections.title: The case for RAG: you pay to re-read, every single time
sections.summary: Long context creates a compute inefficiency that scales with traffic. RAG pays the processing cost once, at indexing time.

sections.title: The case for RAG: attention dilutes as context grows
sections.summary: There is an intuitive assumption that data in the window will be used. Research suggests otherwise.

sections.title: The case for RAG: the infinite dataset
sections.summary: A million-token window sounds enormous until you compare it to an enterprise data lake measured in terabytes.

sections.title: Choosing
sections.summary: Bounded data plus global reasoning favours long context. Unbounded enterprise knowledge still requires a vector database.

glossary.definition: Getting the right external data into a model's prompt at query time, so it can answer about things outside its training data.
The maximum number of tokens a model can process in one call, covering the prompt and the generated output together.
Splitting documents into smaller passages before embedding. Strategies include fixed size, sliding window and recursive splitting on structure.
A model that converts text into a vector whose position encodes meaning, so similar passages sit near each other.
Storage built for fast nearest-neighbour search over embeddings, plus the indexing and sync machinery around it.
Ranking documents by vector similarity to the query rather than by shared keywords, so meaning matches even when wording differs.
When retrieval misses a document that contained the answer. No error is raised — the model simply answers from the wrong material, confidently.
A second-stage model that re-scores retrieved candidates more accurately than vector similarity, usually over a shortlist.
Placing whole documents directly in the prompt and letting the attention mechanism locate what matters, with no retrieval step.
Reusing a provider's processed representation of an identical prompt prefix across requests, cutting the cost of the repeated portion.
A test that plants a known fact at a controlled depth in a long context and checks whether the model can retrieve it.
The degradation in a model's ability to focus on a specific passage as the surrounding context grows.
The fraction of questions for which the correct source passage appears in the top k retrieved results. The ceiling on a RAG system's accuracy.
The unit a model actually processes — a word fragment. Roughly three-quarters of a word for English prose, and much denser for code or JSON.

Knowing When Not to Use AI: AI Agents vs.folder: Knowing When Not to Use AI: AI Agents vs Rules vs ML
Knowing When Not to Use AI: AI Agents vs.title: Choosing the Right Kind of Intelligence: Humans, Rules, ML and Generative AI
Knowing When Not to Use AI: AI Agents vs.subtitle: Learn to match a problem to the cheapest system that can actually solve it, and to recognise when AI is the wrong tool.
Knowing When Not to Use AI: AI Agents vs.overview:
It is easy to fall into using AI for everything. Agent systems are genuinely powerful, and teams are wiring them across their stacks. But AI is not magic and it is not the best solution for every problem. Like any engineering decision, choosing whether to use it — and at what scale — is a trade-off across accuracy, cost, complexity and risk.

Most problems in software and data systems can be solved in one of four ways. Humans, for judgement and accountability. Rules or code, for deterministic logic. Machine learning, for statistical pattern recognition. Generative AI, for flexible reasoning over unstructured input. These are not a ladder you climb from human up to agent. They are distinct options, each with a specific role, and the skill is picking the right one.

The practical stakes are higher than they look. Most failures to reach production do not come from a bad model. They come from choosing the wrong kind of system at the start, and then spending months trying to make it behave like a different one.
key_takeaways: Four options — humans, rules, ML, generative AI — are distinct tools, not rungs on a ladder.
Humans are the right choice for high-stakes, ambiguous, accountability-bearing decisions, and they do not scale.
Rules are the right choice when logic is known, explicit and stable, and when errors are unacceptable.
Rules break when conditions change faster than you can update them, or when the logic grows too complex to write down.
Machine learning fits when patterns exist in structured data but are not obvious enough to encode by hand.
ML is not fire-and-forget: drift monitoring and retraining are permanent operating costs.
Generative AI fits unstructured input, interpretation and synthesis — where flexibility matters more than exactness.
The deciding question for generative AI is how much non-determinism you can tolerate, and the best systems combine all four.

sections.title: Four kinds of intelligence, not a ladder
sections.summary: Humans, rules, machine learning and generative AI are distinct options with distinct roles. Choosing among them is an ordinary engineering trade-off.

sections.title: Humans: judgement, ambiguity and accountability
sections.summary: People handle incomplete and conflicting information, apply ethics and context, and can be held responsible. They are also expensive and do not scale.

sections.title: Rules and code: deterministic logic at scale
sections.summary: When the logic is known, stable and must not be wrong, ordinary code is fast, cheap, testable and completely interpretable.

sections.title: Where rules break down
sections.summary: Rules fail when conditions change constantly or the logic becomes too complex to state. Fraud detection is the standard example.

sections.title: Machine learning: patterns in structured data
sections.summary: Learn the distinguishing pattern from examples instead of stating it. Right when patterns exist but are not obvious enough to encode by hand.

sections.title: What machine learning costs to keep running
sections.summary: Models scale well and behave predictably, and they need monitoring, retraining and an honest account of what they can explain.

sections.title: Generative AI: unstructured input, flexible output
sections.summary: Right when inputs are text or media, tasks need interpretation or transformation, and flexibility matters more than precision.

sections.title: The real question: how much non-determinism can you tolerate?
sections.summary: Generative systems do not guarantee correctness across runs, which makes them hard to test and costly at scale. That tolerance is the deciding criterion.

sections.title: Hybrid systems, and the heuristic
sections.summary: The best systems use all four in combination. 'Make everything agents' was never meant literally.

glossary.definition: One where identical input always produces identical output. Exhaustively testable, and its behaviour is fixed once verified.
Explicit conditional logic written by a person. Fast, cheap, interpretable and correct only for the cases anticipated.
Deriving a predictive function from labelled examples rather than stating it. Suits structured data with patterns too complex to encode by hand.
Gradual degradation in accuracy as the world diverges from the training data. Silent: no error, no code change.
A change in the distribution of incoming features relative to training. Detectable by comparing distributions.
A change in the relationship between inputs and outcomes. Harder to detect, because it requires outcomes that often arrive late.
A measure of how much a feature's distribution has shifted from a baseline. Commonly read as stable below 0.1 and needing retraining above 0.2.
The property that identical input may produce different output across runs. The defining cost of generative systems.
A fixed collection of inputs with known-good outputs, scored repeatedly to catch regressions in a system you cannot assert on exactly.
Using a second model to score an output against a rubric, where the output is too open-ended for a programmatic check.
Identifying which inputs most influenced a prediction. Explains the model's behaviour, never the underlying causality.
An architecture combining humans, rules, ML and generative AI, each applied to the part of the problem it fits.

LLM-as-a-Judge: Direct Assessment, Pairw.folder: LLM-as-a-Judge: Direct Assessment, Pairwise Comparison & the Biases That Skew Both
LLM-as-a-Judge: Direct Assessment, Pairw.title: LLM-as-a-Judge: Direct Assessment, Pairwise Comparison & the Biases That Skew Both
LLM-as-a-Judge: Direct Assessment, Pairw.subtitle: Choose the right judging strategy for your task, and recognise the three biases that make a judge quietly wrong.
LLM-as-a-Judge: Direct Assessment, Pairw.overview:
You have a thousand model outputs — chatbot replies, summaries, generated answers — and you need to know which are good. Labelling them by hand is accurate and impossibly slow. Traditional metrics like BLEU and ROUGE are fast but measure word overlap against a reference answer, which you often do not have and which says little about whether a summary is actually clear.

LLM-as-a-judge fills that gap: a language model evaluates other models' outputs. This lesson covers the two strategies for doing it — direct assessment against a rubric, and pairwise comparison between two candidates — along with what each is good for and how real users choose between them.

It then covers the part that decides whether your judge is trustworthy: the biases. Like human reviewers, LLM judges have systematic blind spots. They can favour whichever answer appeared first, prefer longer answers regardless of content, and rate their own output more highly than others'. None of these makes the approach unusable, but each one produces plausible-looking scores that are wrong in a consistent direction, so you need to know how to detect and correct for them.
key_takeaways: LLM-as-a-judge enables reference-free evaluation: judging quality without a gold-standard answer to compare against.
Direct assessment scores each output independently against a rubric you design; pairwise comparison asks which of two outputs is better.
With multiple candidates, pairwise judgements can be combined by a ranking algorithm to produce an overall ordering.

In IBM's user research on the open-source EvalAssist framework, about half preferred direct assessment for its clarity and control, a quarter preferred pairwise for subjective tasks, and the rest combined both.
The three advantages over traditional metrics are scale, flexibility as your criteria evolve, and the ability to judge nuanced qualities like whether text sounds natural.
Positional bias: the judge favours an output because of where it appeared, not because it is better.
Verbosity bias: the judge treats length as a proxy for quality and prefers longer answers even when they ramble.
Self-enhancement bias: the judge favours output it recognises as its own.
Positional swaps — running the same comparison with the order reversed — detect positional bias directly. Bias means stay vigilant, not that the system is broken.

sections.title: Why traditional metrics run out
sections.summary: Manual labelling does not scale and word-overlap metrics need a reference answer they cannot always have.

sections.title: Strategy one: direct assessment
sections.summary: Design a rubric and score each output against it independently, one at a time.

sections.title: Strategy two: pairwise comparison
sections.summary: Instead of a standalone label, ask which of two outputs is better — then rank many outputs from the accumulated comparisons.

sections.title: Which strategy do people actually choose?
sections.summary: User research on the open-source EvalAssist framework found the split was roughly half direct assessment, a quarter pairwise, and the rest a combination — with the choice depending on both task and user.

sections.title: Why use an LLM judge: scale, flexibility, nuance
sections.summary: It handles volume, it adapts as your criteria shift, and it can evaluate qualities no overlap metric reaches.

sections.title: The three biases that skew a judge
sections.summary: Positional, verbosity, and self-enhancement bias each make a judge favour outputs for reasons unrelated to quality.

sections.title: Catching bias with positional swaps
sections.summary: Run the same comparison twice with the options in reverse order; if the verdict flips, the judgement was driven by position rather than content.

Judging an output on its own merits, without needing a gold-standard answer to compare it against.
A judging strategy where each output is scored independently against a rubric you designed.
A judging strategy where two outputs are shown together and the judge picks which is better.
The criterion being evaluated plus the set of options the judge may return.
A method for converting many individual pairwise verdicts into an overall ordering of all candidates.
Traditional text metrics that score an output by how much its wording overlaps with a reference answer.
A judge favouring an output because of the position it appeared in rather than its content.
A judge favouring longer outputs regardless of quality, treating length as a signal of thoroughness.
A judge rating its own generated output more highly than others', independent of actual quality.
Re-running a pairwise comparison with the two options in reverse order to test whether the verdict was driven by position.
IBM's open-sourced evaluation framework, used in the user research on how people choose between judging strategies.

MCP vs Skills: Which Is Right for Your A.folder: MCP vs Skills: Which Is Right for Your AI Agent and LLMs?
MCP vs Skills: Which Is Right for Your A.title: MCP vs Skills: Two Ways to Extend an LLM's Context
MCP vs Skills: Which Is Right for Your A.subtitle: Understand when to wire an LLM to live external data with MCP, and when to teach it a repeatable procedure with a skill.
MCP vs Skills: Which Is Right for Your A.topic: AI agents and LLM context engineering
MCP vs Skills: Which Is Right for Your A.overview:
A large language model only knows what it saw during training, plus whatever text you put in its context window at request time. Getting a useful answer out of it is less about the wording of your question and more about what surrounding information you supply — this is context engineering, and it is broader than prompt engineering. Two complementary mechanisms have emerged for supplying that context at scale: the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and skills.

MCP standardizes how an LLM-based application talks to external systems — CRMs, databases, internal APIs — so the model can fetch or act on live data through a scoped, authenticated interface instead of you hand-rolling API glue for every tool. Skills solve a different problem: they package a reusable, repeatable procedure — a way of doing a task the same way every time — as a small bundle of instructions (and optionally scripts and resources) that the model loads into its context only when the task calls for it.

This lesson explains both mechanisms, shows the shape of a real MCP tool call and a real skill file, and gives you a rule of thumb for choosing between them or using both together.
key_takeaways: An LLM answers well only when its context window contains the right information, not just a well-phrased question — this is the difference between prompt engineering and context engineering.

MCP (Model Context Protocol) standardizes how an LLM-based application calls external services: it turns a service's API into an LLM-readable set of tools, and it handles scoped, authenticated access to that service.
Without MCP, giving a model raw API documentation and a token and hoping it calls the API correctly is fragile and unauditable.
MCP does not make an LLM's behavior repeatable — LLMs are non-deterministic, so even with the same data source, output formatting and process can vary run to run.
A skill is a packaged, reusable set of instructions (typically a markdown file plus metadata, optionally with scripts and resources) that teaches the model to perform a task the same way every time.
Skills are auto-loaded into the context window only when relevant, so they don't bloat every request with instructions the current task doesn't need.

Choose MCP when the agent needs controlled, permissioned access to real-time external data. Choose a skill when you need a lightweight, repeatable way of doing something the model doesn't already know how to do consistently.
MCP and skills are complementary, not competing: an agent can use MCP to fetch live CRM data and a skill to guarantee that data is always formatted and processed the same way.

sections.title: From prompt engineering to context engineering
sections.summary: An LLM is a pattern-matching system trained on huge amounts of text; the quality of its answer depends on what extra information you give it beyond the question itself.

sections.title: MCP: a standard interface between an LLM and external services
sections.summary: The Model Context Protocol standardizes how an AI application calls external data sources and services, so the model doesn't need raw API docs and a bare token to get live data.

sections.title: What MCP doesn't solve: repeatable, non-deterministic behavior
sections.summary: LLMs are non-deterministic, so even with reliable access to live data via MCP, the model can format or process that data differently each time unless it's told a fixed procedure to follow.

sections.title: Skills: packaging a repeatable procedure the model can auto-load
sections.summary: A skill is a reusable bundle — a markdown file with metadata, optionally packaged with scripts and resources in a folder — that teaches the model to do a specific task the same way every time, loaded into context only when needed.

sections.title: Choosing MCP, skills, or both
sections.summary: Reach for MCP when the agent needs controlled, permissioned access to real-time external data; reach for a skill when you need a lightweight, repeatable way to perform a task the model doesn't already do consistently.

glossary.definition: The span of text an LLM can see at once when generating a response, including the prompt, any supplied data, and prior conversation.
Crafting the wording, role, and task of a request to an LLM to shape its response.
Deciding what information — data, formatting rules, tool output — needs to be present in the model's context window for it to answer correctly, beyond just the wording of the prompt.
A standardized protocol that lets an AI application call external services and data sources through a common, LLM-readable interface, handling both request translation and authentication.
A server that implements MCP for a specific service, exposing a set of typed tools to the AI application and translating tool calls into that service's real API requests.
An access credential limited to exactly the permissions (e.g. read-only, or write access to one resource type) that a given task needs, rather than a broad, all-access credential.

A reusable, packaged set of instructions — typically a markdown file with metadata, optionally bundled with scripts and resources — that teaches an LLM to perform a specific task the same way every time, loaded into context only when relevant.
Producing different outputs on different runs even given the same input, which is a property of how LLMs generate text and why unenforced instructions don't guarantee repeatable results.
The behavior where an AI application matches the current task against each available skill's description and pulls only the matching skill's instructions into the context window.
A lightweight remote-procedure-call protocol encoded in JSON, used by MCP to structure requests like tools/list and tools/call between client and server.

Multi-Agent Architectures That Ship: Fiv.folder: Multi-Agent Architectures That Ship: Five Patterns, Three Roles & Validation Contracts
Multi-Agent Architectures That Ship: Fiv.title: Multi-Agent Architectures That Ship: Five Patterns, Three Roles & Validation Contracts
Multi-Agent Architectures That Ship: Fiv.subtitle: Assemble agent teams that run for days — by separating who builds from who verifies, defining 'done' before any code exists, and putting the right model in each seat.
Multi-Agent Architectures That Ship: Fiv.overview:
The bottleneck in software engineering is no longer intelligence — it is human attention. A team may have fifty features in the backlog and models capable of implementing all of them, but only enough bandwidth to supervise a few per day, because every task needs attention and every commit needs review. The interesting question becomes: what if a human decides what to build, and a system figures out how?

Multi-agent research is a mess of competing frameworks and terminology, so this lesson starts with a taxonomy that cuts through it — five communication patterns from which every multi-agent system is assembled. It then walks through one production architecture built from four of them, called missions, whose longest run lasted sixteen days.

The surprises are where the value is. Parallelism, the obvious way to go faster, made things worse and was abandoned for serial execution with narrow internal parallelism. Tests written by the agent that wrote the code turn out to confirm decisions rather than catch bugs, which forced validation to be redesigned around a contract written before implementation. And the whole orchestration lives in roughly 700 lines of prompt text rather than a state machine, specifically so the system improves when models improve instead of being obsoleted by them.
key_takeaways: Five patterns compose every multi-agent system: delegation, creator-verifier, direct communication, negotiation, and broadcast.
Direct communication (agents DMing each other with no coordinator) is the one to avoid — state fragments and there is no single source of truth.
Separate the agent that builds from the agent that verifies: the author has a cost bias toward its own code working, exactly why humans do code review.
A validation contract, written during planning before any code, defines correctness independently of implementation — often hundreds of assertions, each feature owning one or more.
Tests written after implementation are shaped by the code rather than the intent, so they confirm decisions instead of catching bugs.

Validate behaviour, not just code: a QA-style validator drives the running application through computer use, and that real-world execution — not token generation — consumes most of a mission's wall-clock time.
Structured handoffs (what was done, what was left, commands run with exit codes, issues found) are what let the system self-heal at milestone boundaries.
Serial execution with targeted read-only parallelism beat parallel workers: coordination overhead ate the speed gains while the error rate rose.

Planning, implementation, and validation reward different model strengths, and no single provider is best at all three — being model-agnostic means you are not capped by one family's weakest capability.
Keep orchestration in prompts and skills rather than a hard-coded state machine, so every model improvement makes the system better instead of obsolete.

sections.summary: Models can already handle the whole backlog; what runs out is the human bandwidth to supervise them.

sections.title: The five multi-agent communication patterns
sections.summary: Delegation, creator-verifier, direct communication, negotiation, and broadcast — the primitives every framework is built from.

sections.title: Missions: four patterns in one workflow, three roles
sections.summary: Orchestrator plans, workers implement, validators verify — an ecosystem communicating through structured handoffs and shared state, not one long agent session.

sections.title: Validation contracts: define 'done' before writing code
sections.summary: Tests written after implementation are shaped by the code rather than the intent, so they confirm decisions instead of catching bugs.

sections.title: Two validators, adversarial by design
sections.summary: A scrutiny validator runs the suite and spawns per-feature code review; a user-testing validator drives the live application like a QA engineer.

sections.title: Structured handoffs and self-healing
sections.summary: A worker does not just report 'done' — it writes down what happened, and the system corrects course at milestone boundaries.

sections.title: Serial execution beats parallelism
sections.summary: Ten agents did not give ten times the throughput — they conflicted, duplicated work, and made inconsistent decisions until coordination overhead ate the gains.

sections.title: The right model in each seat
sections.summary: Planning wants slow careful reasoning, implementation wants fast code fluency, validation wants precise instruction following — and no one provider is best at all three.

sections.title: Beating the bitter lesson: prompts, not state machines
sections.summary: Keep orchestration logic in text so the next model release improves the system instead of obsoleting it.

sections.title: Production reality, and what it unlocks
sections.summary: A Slack clone built end to end: 60% of time and tokens on implementation, validation never passing first time, and half the final codebase being tests.

glossary.definition: A long-running multi-agent workflow: you approve a plan, then an ecosystem of agents executes it for hours or days via structured handoffs and shared state.
One agent spawning another to do a scoped piece of work and return a result — the simplest multi-agent pattern.
Separating the agent that builds something from the agent that checks it, because the author is biased toward its own work succeeding.
Agents messaging each other with no central coordinator. Avoided here because state fragments and no single source of truth exists.
Agents coordinating over a shared resource such as an API or a region of the codebase, ideally finding a positive-sum outcome.
One agent distributing information to many — status, new context, shared constraints — to keep a long run coherent.
The planning role: interrogates requirements and produces features, milestones, and the validation contract.
The implementation role: takes one feature with clean context, implements it, and commits so the next worker inherits a working codebase.
The verification role: an agent that has never seen the code, checking it against the contract — adversarial by design.
A set of assertions defining correctness, written during planning before any code, with each feature assigned the assertions it must satisfy.
The static validator: test suite, type checking, lints, plus a dedicated code review agent per completed feature.
The behavioural validator: spawns the running application and drives it via computer use, checking whole functional flows.
A worker's written record of what it completed, what it left undone, the commands and exit codes, issues found, and whether it followed procedure.
The checkpoint after a group of features where validators run, handoffs are reviewed, and corrective work is scoped.
The skill of modelling how different models behave and fail, and deliberately assigning each to the role it suits.
The observation that general methods leveraging more compute tend to beat hand-engineered structure — hence keeping orchestration in prompts rather than code.

RAG vs Fine-Tuning vs Prompt Engineering.folder: RAG vs Fine-Tuning vs Prompt Engineering: Optimizing AI Models
RAG vs Fine-Tuning vs Prompt Engineering.title: RAG, Fine-Tuning and Prompt Engineering: Choosing How to Improve an LLM
RAG vs Fine-Tuning vs Prompt Engineering.subtitle: Know which of the three levers to pull, what each one actually costs, and how to layer them.
RAG vs Fine-Tuning vs Prompt Engineering.overview:
A language model's knowledge is frozen at the moment training stopped, and it lives inside the weights rather than in any file you can open. Ask about something newer than the cutoff, or something private to your organisation, and the model has nothing to work from — so it guesses, fluently.

Three techniques address this, and the useful way to tell them apart is by where in the stack they intervene. RAG changes what reaches the model at query time. Fine-tuning changes the weights. Prompt engineering changes the request. That is the whole taxonomy: retrieval supplies facts, fine-tuning installs behaviour, prompting redirects capability that is already present.

They are not competitors, and picking between them is mostly a matter of naming what is actually missing. Missing facts point at retrieval. Wrong behaviour, tone or format points at fine-tuning. A capable model answering a badly specified question points at the prompt. Production systems normally use all three, layered.
key_takeaways: Parametric knowledge is fixed at the training cutoff — anything newer or private has to arrive through the prompt.
RAG is retrieve, augment, generate: the weights are untouched, only the model's input changes.
Retrieval matches meaning rather than words, because both the query and the corpus are converted to vectors and compared geometrically.
RAG's price is latency on every single query plus an embedding-and-indexing pipeline you have to keep in sync forever.
Fine-tuning updates weights from input–output pairs, so behaviour is baked in, inference stays fast, and no vector database is needed.
Fine-tuning's price is thousands of curated examples, GPU time, a full retraining round for every update, and the risk of catastrophic forgetting.
Prompt engineering steers attention toward patterns already in the weights: instant and free, and structurally incapable of adding knowledge.
Sequence the work cheapest-first — prompt, then retrieval, then fine-tuning — because each stage produces the evaluation the next one needs.

sections.title: Why the same question gets different answers from different models
sections.summary: Everything a model knows sits in its weights, frozen when training stopped. Every improvement technique is a way of working around that one fact.

sections.title: RAG: retrieval, augmentation, generation
sections.summary: The acronym is the architecture. Find relevant text, paste it into the prompt, then answer from it — with the model itself never modified.

sections.title: Embeddings: finding documents that share no words with the query
sections.summary: Both the question and every document become vectors, so relevance is measured as closeness in space rather than overlap in vocabulary.

sections.title: What RAG costs: latency per query, infrastructure forever
sections.summary: Retrieval is not free. It adds a round trip to every single request and a pipeline you have to operate indefinitely.

sections.title: Fine-tuning: continuing training on a narrow dataset
sections.summary: Take a model that already has broad competence and keep training it on examples of the behaviour you want.

sections.title: How the weights actually move
sections.summary: Supervised fine-tuning is a loss on predicted tokens, backpropagated into the weights, repeated across the dataset.

sections.title: The bill for fine-tuning: data, GPUs, maintenance and forgetting
sections.summary: Four costs — and the fourth, losing general ability while gaining specialised ability, is the one that catches teams out.

sections.title: Prompt engineering: aiming attention at capability that is already there
sections.summary: A prompt is not a request so much as a set of conditions. Change it and you change which learned patterns dominate the output.

sections.title: Where prompt engineering stops
sections.summary: No phrasing adds information the weights never held, and finding a good prompt is empirical rather than derivable.

sections.title: Combining all three
sections.summary: In production these are layers rather than alternatives, each covering a gap the other two leave open.

glossary.definition: Information encoded implicitly in a model's weights during training. It cannot be listed, edited or deleted directly — only probed by asking the model.
The date at which a model's training data ends. Nothing after it exists in the weights, no matter how significant.
Searching a corpus for passages relevant to a query, inserting them into the prompt, and generating an answer from them. The model itself is never modified.
A fixed-length list of numbers representing a piece of text, arranged so that texts with similar meaning produce nearby vectors.
The cosine of the angle between two vectors, used to score relevance. It ignores magnitude, so a long document and a short phrase about the same thing still match.
A store built for fast nearest-neighbour search over embeddings. It is the piece of infrastructure RAG obliges you to run and keep in sync.
Splitting documents into passages before embedding them. Chunk size and boundaries strongly affect whether retrieval can find anything.
Constraining a model to answer from supplied text rather than from memory, usually by instruction. It is what makes a retrieved answer checkable.
Continuing training on a pre-trained model with a focused dataset, so the desired behaviour ends up stored in the weights.
Fine-tuning on explicit input–output pairs, where each example shows a request and the response the model should have produced.
The algorithm that works out how much each weight contributed to the error, so the optimiser knows which direction to move it.
The standard training objective for language models: it is large when the model assigned low probability to the token that was actually correct.
Loss of general capability during specialised training, as the weights drift away from the configuration that supported it.
Parameter-efficient fine-tuning: freeze the base model and train small adapter matrices instead. Cheaper to train, cheaper to store, and reversible.
The component in each transformer layer that weighs parts of the input against one another, deciding what influences the output most.
Including worked examples in the prompt to demonstrate the desired output rather than describing it.
The maximum amount of text a model can attend to at once. It bounds how much retrieved material a RAG system can supply.
Running a trained model to produce output, as opposed to training it. RAG adds work here; fine-tuning moves work out of it.

RAG's Evolution: From Simple Retrieval t.folder: RAG's Evolution: From Simple Retrieval to Agentic AI
RAG's Evolution: From Simple Retrieval t.title: From Inverted Indices to Agentic RAG: How Retrieval Grew Up
RAG's Evolution: From Simple Retrieval t.subtitle: Follow information retrieval from keyword matching to systems that decide for themselves what to look at.
RAG's Evolution: From Simple Retrieval t.overview:
Search engines did not get smarter overnight. Information retrieval grew up one step at a time, and each step was a response to a specific, nameable failure of the step before it. Keyword indices could not handle synonyms. Semantic search could not handle exact identifiers. Static RAG pipelines could not adapt when one retrieval was not enough.

That progression is worth knowing in detail, because almost every retrieval system in production today is sitting at one of these stages, and its problems are the documented problems of that stage. A team fighting recall issues with better embeddings is often at the point where hybrid retrieval was invented. A team whose RAG works on simple questions and collapses on multi-hop ones is at the point where agentic retrieval was invented.

The endpoint so far is retrieval as a tool inside a reasoning loop, rather than a fixed step ahead of one. The agent decides whether to search, where, what to ask, and when it has enough. As the video puts it: the hardest part is not generation, it is deciding what to look at.
key_takeaways: An inverted index maps terms to the documents containing them, which is what makes keyword search fast.
BM25 ranks by term frequency, inverse document frequency and document length, and remains a strong baseline decades on.
Lexical search treats words as symbols, so synonyms, ambiguity and intent are invisible to it.
Embeddings are learned from context, which is why 'espresso' lands near 'coffee' and far from 'house'.
Hybrid retrieval combines lexical precision with semantic recall because each covers the other's failures.
LLMs predict likely tokens rather than retrieving facts, so their knowledge is frozen and unattributable.
Naive RAG is linear — embed offline, retrieve once, generate — and is only ever as good as that single retrieval.
Agentic RAG makes retrieval a tool invoked during reasoning, so the system can iterate, verify and stop when it has enough.

sections.title: Keyword search: inverted indices and ranking
sections.summary: The earliest systems answered one question — where does this word appear — using a mapping from terms to documents, then ranked the hits by statistical importance.

sections.title: Where lexical matching breaks
sections.summary: It treats words as symbols, not as meaning. Synonyms, ambiguity and intent are invisible.

sections.title: Semantic search: meaning as geometry
sections.summary: Represent text as vectors in a high-dimensional space where similar concepts sit close together, and relevance becomes distance.

sections.title: Hybrid retrieval: precision and recall together
sections.summary: Semantic search did not replace keyword search. Systems combining both emerged because each covers the other's failures exactly.

sections.title: LLMs predict — they do not retrieve
sections.summary: A language model returns the most likely continuation based on learned patterns. It has no index, no sources and no notion of looking something up.

sections.title: Naive RAG: the linear pipeline
sections.summary: Search for relevant documents, augment the prompt with them, generate the answer. Simple, effective, and only as good as one retrieval.

sections.title: Advanced RAG: rerankers, query rewriting, hybrid
sections.summary: Within a short period the simple concept accumulated real machinery — but the pipeline stayed fixed.

sections.title: Agentic RAG: retrieval as a tool inside reasoning
sections.summary: Retrieval stops being a fixed step before the answer and becomes something the system invokes, repeats and stops as part of thinking.

glossary.definition: A mapping from each term to the documents containing it — the reverse of the natural document-to-terms direction, which is what makes lookup fast.
Term frequency times inverse document frequency: a term matters more if it is frequent in this document and rare across the corpus.
The standard lexical ranking function, refining TF-IDF with saturating term frequency and document-length normalisation.
Retrieval by literal term matching. Precise on exact strings, blind to synonyms and intent.
Retrieval by proximity between embeddings, so documents match on meaning even when they share no words.
A high-dimensional vector representing text, learned so that items appearing in similar contexts occupy similar positions.
Running lexical and semantic retrieval together and fusing the results, since each covers the other's characteristic failures.
Combining several ranked lists by summing 1/(k + rank) per document, avoiding the need to make incompatible scores comparable.
An embedding model that encodes query and document separately, allowing the corpus to be indexed in advance.
A model that reads query and document together and scores the pair. More accurate than a bi-encoder and too slow to run over a full corpus.
A second-stage scorer, usually a cross-encoder, applied to a retrieved shortlist to reorder it more accurately.
Reformulating a short or conversational question into a fuller standalone query before retrieval, to improve recall.
The original linear pipeline: retrieve once, augment the prompt, generate. No feedback and no second attempt.
Retrieval invoked as a tool during reasoning, so the system decides whether, where and how often to search, and when it has enough.
A question whose answer requires a second lookup that depends on the result of the first. Beyond the reach of single-shot retrieval.

Synthetic Data Generation for Smarter AI.folder: Synthetic Data Generation for Smarter AI Workflows
Synthetic Data Generation for Smarter AI.title: Synthetic Data Generation for Smarter AI Workflows
Synthetic Data Generation for Smarter AI.subtitle: Turn a handful of real examples into a large, validated training set without hand-labeling everything yourself.
Synthetic Data Generation for Smarter AI.overview:
Suppose you want a chatbot that can answer questions from a specific research paper. A base language model was not trained on that paper, so it cannot reliably answer questions about it. Fine-tuning could fix this, but fine-tuning needs training examples, and a single paper does not contain enough of them. This is the data problem behind almost every domain-specific AI project: the raw source material exists, but it is not in a form a model can learn from, and there usually is not much of it.

The fix is a three-stage pipeline. First, extract structured content from unstructured documents. Second, turn a small amount of that structured content into a handful of hand-written question-and-answer examples, called seed data. Third, use a model to expand that seed data into a much larger set of new, similar examples: synthetic data. The word "synthetic" does not mean fake or low-quality here — it means generated rather than manually written, while still being checked for accuracy against the source.

This overview walks through each stage, the open source tools that implement them (Docling for extraction, SDGHub for generation), the validation checks that keep synthetic data trustworthy, and the practical reasons teams reach for this approach: privacy, class balance, and reproducible pipelines.
key_takeaways: Models cannot learn directly from raw documents; unstructured text, tables, and equations must first be converted into structured data.
A small set of hand-written question-and-answer pairs, called seed data, teaches a generation model the pattern and style to imitate.
Synthetic data generation is a pipeline, not a single API call: it generates candidate examples, transforms them, and validates them before they are used.
Validation checks synthetic examples for faithfulness to the source, relevance to the question, and diversity across the dataset.
Generation pipelines can run entirely inside your own environment, connecting to local or self-hosted models, so source data never has to leave it.
Synthetic data lets you preserve privacy, balance rare classes, and augment thin domains without collecting more real-world data.
Because the pipeline is generate-validate-deploy on repeatable steps, the resulting dataset is reproducible — a requirement for most enterprise AI workflows.

sections.title: Why you can't just point a model at a PDF
sections.summary: A model can't learn from a document directly, and even structured content usually isn't enough of it to shift a base model's weights.

sections.title: Extracting structured context from raw documents
sections.summary: Tools like Docling turn PDFs and scans into structured data — sections, headings, tables — using OCR and parsing, which is the first step before any generation happens.

sections.title: Generating synthetic data from seed examples
sections.summary: Once seed data exists, a generation model studies its patterns and produces new, similar question-and-answer pairs at scale — this is synthetic data generation.

sections.title: Validating synthetic data before you trust it
sections.summary: Generated examples are checked for faithfulness, relevance, and diversity, and the whole flow can run locally against your own model endpoint so source data never leaves your environment.

sections.title: Why control over the data matters
sections.summary: Synthetic data generation isn't just about producing more text — it gives you privacy preservation, class balancing, and a reproducible pipeline you can run before every deployment.

glossary.definition: A small, hand-written set of example question-and-answer pairs that demonstrates the correct pattern and style for a model to imitate when generating more examples.
New data examples produced by a model rather than collected from the real world, generated to follow the statistical pattern of a smaller real dataset.
Software that converts images of text, such as a scanned page, into machine-readable text characters.
A validation check on whether a generated answer's claims are actually supported by the source document, as opposed to invented.
An open source tool that converts PDFs and scanned documents into structured data — sections, headings, tables — using OCR and parsing.
An open source project that runs synthetic data generation flows: pipelines that generate, transform, and validate synthetic examples.
An API that accepts requests in the same format as OpenAI's API, letting tools switch between providers (self-hosted, Claude, etc.) without changing code.
Continuing to train an existing base model on a smaller, task-specific dataset so its weights shift toward that task.

The Four Types of Memory Every AI Agent.folder: The Four Types of Memory Every AI Agent Needs
The Four Types of Memory Every AI Agent.title: The Four Types of Agent Memory: Working, Semantic, Procedural, Episodic
The Four Types of Memory Every AI Agent.subtitle: Know which store to reach for, what each costs you in context, and why forgetting is the hard part.
The Four Types of Memory Every AI Agent.overview:
A language model is stateless. Every capability that looks like memory is something the surrounding system built, and the useful question is not whether your agent has memory but which kind, held where, loaded when.

The CoALA framework — Cognitive Architectures for Language Agents, from a Princeton research team — names four types, and they map cleanly onto how people remember. Working memory is what is active right now. Semantic memory is what you know. Procedural memory is what you know how to do. Episodic memory is what happened to you before.

The distinction is worth more than a taxonomy, because the four differ in exactly the ways that matter to an implementation: whether they survive the session, whether they cost context tokens continuously or only on demand, who writes to them, and how they go stale. Working memory is volatile and always loaded. Semantic memory is stable and usually always loaded. Procedural memory is loaded on demand. Episodic memory accumulates by itself, and that is the one that turns into an engineering problem.
key_takeaways: Models are stateless — every kind of agent memory is machinery the surrounding system provides.
CoALA names four types: working, semantic, procedural and episodic, mirroring human memory.
Working memory is the context window: fast, always present, volatile, and capped in size.
Semantic memory is what the agent knows in general, and in production it is often just Markdown files rather than a vector database.
Procedural memory is how the agent does things, packaged as skills with step-by-step instructions.
Progressive disclosure keeps procedural memory affordable: advertise a short index, load the full instructions only on a match.
Episodic memory is distilled experience, not saved transcripts — the compression is what makes it useful.
Forgetting is the hardest part, because staleness and obsolescence have to be decided in code rather than felt.

sections.title: Human memory as the map
sections.summary: Four kinds of remembering that people do without noticing, which turn out to be four separate engineering problems.

sections.title: CoALA: naming the four
sections.summary: A framework from a Princeton research team that maps out the distinct memory types an agent needs.

sections.title: Working memory: the context window
sections.summary: Everything the agent can see right now — the conversation, the system instructions, whatever has been loaded into the prompt.

sections.title: Semantic memory: what the agent knows
sections.summary: The knowledge base — facts, rules, conventions, documentation. In production it is frequently just Markdown.

sections.title: Procedural memory: how the agent does things
sections.summary: Skills — a folder with a Markdown file describing what the skill does and the steps to perform it.

sections.title: Progressive disclosure
sections.summary: The agent advertises a lightweight index, loads full instructions on a match, and pulls in supporting files only during execution.

sections.title: Episodic memory: what happened before
sections.summary: The record of past interactions and decisions, and what was learned from them — distilled rather than stored whole.

sections.title: Forgetting is an engineering problem
sections.summary: What do you delete? When does something become obsolete? People forget effortlessly; agents have to be told.

sections.title: Not every agent needs all four
sections.summary: Match the memory architecture to what the agent actually does. Most need fewer types than the taxonomy suggests.

glossary.definition: Cognitive Architectures for Language Agents, a framework from a Princeton research team that identifies four memory types agents need.
The context window: the conversation, instructions and loaded data the agent can see right now. Fast, volatile and capped.
What the agent knows in general — facts, rules, conventions and documentation. Often a Markdown file loaded at session start.
How the agent performs a task: ordered, step-by-step instructions, packaged as a skill.
The record of past sessions and what was learned from them, kept as distilled notes rather than whole transcripts.
The maximum text a model can process in one call. It bounds working memory and everything loaded into it.
Advertising skills by a short description, loading full instructions only on a match, and supporting files only during execution.
The lightweight list of skill names and descriptions the agent always sees — roughly a hundred tokens per skill.
The Markdown file defining a skill: what it does, when to use it, and the steps to perform it.
A project-root Markdown file holding architecture, conventions, commands and prohibitions, loaded at the start of every session.
Compressing a session into a few durable conclusions worth remembering, instead of storing the transcript.
Dropping a whole class of memories when the context they belonged to ends — a project archived, an account closed.
An agent that maps an input directly to an action with no persistence, needing only working memory.
A stored memory that has become false. Worse than no memory, because it displaces correct behaviour rather than merely omitting it.

The Promptware Kill Chain: How Prompt In.folder: The Promptware Kill Chain: How Prompt Injection Becomes AI Malware
The Promptware Kill Chain: How Prompt In.title: The Promptware Kill Chain: How Prompt Injection Becomes AI Malware
The Promptware Kill Chain: How Prompt In.subtitle: Understand how a single malicious prompt can escalate into a full system compromise, and where you can break the chain.
The Promptware Kill Chain: How Prompt In.overview:
Malware has always had recognizable categories: ransomware locks your files for payment, spyware quietly exfiltrates data, adware bombards you with unwanted content. Promptware is the newest entry in that list, and it works differently because it does not exploit a bug in code. It exploits a structural property of large language models: they do not separate instructions from data. Everything a model reads, whether it is a system prompt, a user message, an email, or a calendar invite, is just tokens, and the model will treat authoritative-sounding text as an instruction no matter where it came from.

Security researcher Bruce Schneier and his co-authors describe a 'promptware kill chain': a sequence of stages, borrowed from traditional cybersecurity's kill-chain model, that traces how a single injected prompt can grow into data theft, financial fraud, or a self-propagating infection across every tool an AI agent can reach. This lesson walks through each stage of that chain, in order, and ends with the defensive posture Schneier recommends: zero trust, applied to AI agents themselves.

The point is not that any one stage is exotic. It's that each stage is individually plausible, and once a few of them chain together, an AI agent with real permissions becomes a much more dangerous foothold than a single leaked password.
key_takeaways: Promptware is malware where the payload is natural-language text fed to a generative AI system, not compiled code.
LLMs do not have a hard boundary between instructions and data; any tokens the model reads, including third-party content it summarizes or looks up, can function as a command.
The kill chain runs: initial access, privilege escalation (jailbreaking), reconnaissance, persistence, command and control, lateral movement, and finally action on objective.
Reconnaissance happens after compromise in promptware, unlike in traditional malware where attackers scope a target before breaking in.

Persistence is possible because agents write to and read from long-term memory such as RAG databases, email archives, and chat history; a planted instruction gets re-executed every time that memory is referenced.
Because agents are interconnected with email, calendars, smart devices, and other agents, a single injected prompt can move laterally and spread like a virus through everything the agent can touch.
You cannot patch prompt injection away, because it exploits how LLMs fundamentally process input, so defense means assuming breach (zero trust) and limiting what a compromised agent can do.
Breaking the kill chain at any single link, such as constraining tool access or detecting unexpected persistence, stops the attack from reaching its objective even if initial access succeeds.

sections.title: What promptware is, and why LLMs are structurally vulnerable to it
sections.summary: Promptware is a malware execution model where the payload is a prompt, made possible because LLMs process instructions and data as the same kind of token stream.

sections.title: Stage 1: Initial access via prompt injection
sections.summary: Attackers get their payload into the system either directly, by typing it into the prompt, or indirectly, by planting it in content the AI will later consume.

sections.title: Stage 2: Privilege escalation through jailbreaking
sections.summary: Once inside, the attacker manipulates the model into bypassing its safety alignment, effectively gaining administrator-level control over its reasoning.

sections.title: Stage 3: Reconnaissance happens after the compromise
sections.summary: Unlike traditional attacks, promptware recon comes after initial access: the attacker gets the compromised model to reveal its own tools, APIs, plugins, and permissions.

sections.title: Stage 4: Persistence through the agent's own memory
sections.summary: A chatbot's context is normally ephemeral, but agents that read and write long-term memory can be made to re-execute a planted instruction every time that memory is referenced.

sections.title: Stage 5: Command and control (C2) via the agent's own internet access
sections.summary: Once persistence is established, the attacker can use the LLM's own ability to browse or fetch external content as a remote control channel, turning a fixed attack into an ongoing one.

sections.title: Stage 6: Lateral movement across connected systems
sections.summary: AI agents are often connected to email, calendars, smart devices, and other agents; a foothold in one can spread to all of them, the way a virus spreads through contacts.

sections.title: Stage 7: Action on objective — the real-world payoff
sections.summary: The kill chain's endpoint is real-world impact: data theft, financial fraud, or arbitrary code execution, achieved through reasoning rather than a traditional exploit.

sections.title: Defense: assume breach and break the chain with zero trust
sections.summary: Prompt injection cannot be eliminated at the source, so defenses should assume initial access will happen and focus on limiting what a compromised agent can do at every later stage.

glossary.definition: A malware execution model where the malicious payload is a prompt fed into a generative AI chatbot or agent, rather than compiled code.

Getting an AI model to follow attacker-supplied instructions by including them in text the model processes, either typed directly (direct injection) or hidden in content the model later reads (indirect injection).
A step-by-step model describing the stages of a cyberattack, from initial access through to achieving the attacker's final objective.
Manipulating an AI model into bypassing its safety alignment and behavioral rules, the AI-specific equivalent of privilege escalation.
Turning limited access into broader, more powerful access over a system; in promptware this means gaining effective control over the model's reasoning via jailbreaking.
A jailbreak technique that reframes a disallowed request inside a legitimate-sounding role or context (e.g. 'as a chemistry student') to get the model to comply.

Gathering information about a target system's structure and weaknesses; in the promptware kill chain this happens after compromise, when the model is manipulated into revealing its own tools and permissions.
An attacker's ability to make a compromise outlast the original session by embedding it in data the system will read again later, such as long-term memory.
A technique where a model retrieves relevant documents from an external database and includes them in its context before generating a response.
A channel an attacker uses to send new instructions to an already-compromised system after the initial breach, turning a fixed attack into an ongoing, remotely directed one.
Spreading a compromise from the system initially breached to other connected systems, such as an agent's email, calendar, or smart-home integrations.
The final stage of a kill chain: the attacker's actual real-world goal, such as data theft, financial fraud, or arbitrary code execution.
A security posture that assumes an attacker may already be inside the system and designs defenses accordingly, rather than relying solely on keeping attackers out.
A control point placed in front of an AI model that inspects prompts and can detect or reject suspicious ones before they reach the model.

The Three Levels of LLM Evals: Unit Test.folder: The Three Levels of LLM Evals: Unit Tests, Aligned Judges & AB Testing
The Three Levels of LLM Evals: Unit Test.title: The Three Levels of LLM Evals: Unit Tests, Aligned Judges & A/B Testing
The Three Levels of LLM Evals: Unit Test.subtitle: Build an evaluation-driven workflow — assertions on every change, human-aligned judges every week, and A/B tests on major releases.
The Three Levels of LLM Evals: Unit Test.overview:
Reports suggest a large share of AI projects fail to reach production — Gartner has projected that 40% of agentic AI projects will be cancelled by 2027, and an MIT figure of 95% of generative AI pilots failing has circulated widely. Whether or not those exact numbers hold, the pattern behind them is real: teams build something that works on the happy path, ship it, and then have no systematic way to find out what is going wrong or to fix it without breaking something else.

This lesson lays out the engineering answer. It starts with the three core challenges that make LLM development different from ordinary software — you do not understand the data flowing through your system, you cannot fully specify what you want in a prompt, and behaviour is inconsistent across near-identical inputs. It then presents evaluations organised into three levels of increasing cost: unit tests you run on every change, human and model evaluation you run weekly, and A/B tests you run on major releases.

The centrepiece is the alignment process: how to build an LLM judge that actually agrees with a domain expert, measured by an agreement score you drive upward through iteration. This is the step nearly everyone skips in favour of an off-the-shelf tool with a pretty dashboard, and skipping it is what produces confident metrics that mean nothing.
key_takeaways: Three core challenges define LLM development: not understanding your data at scale, the gap between what you want and what you can specify, and inconsistent behaviour on similar inputs.
An eval is a systematic measurement of quality — a single metric for a specific aspect. One system has many evals.
Evals are operationalised three ways: background monitoring, real-time guardrails, and improvement tooling for labelling and fine-tuning data.
The analyze → measure → improve cycle is the working loop: collect and categorise failures, turn them into metrics, then change prompts, models, or architecture.
Level 1 is unit tests — fast, cheap assertions run on every code and prompt change.
Level 2 is human and model evaluation — systematic review run weekly or bi-weekly. Humans must come first; the LLM judge is aligned to them, never the reverse.
Level 3 is A/B testing with real users, reserved for major releases because of its cost.
The agreement score between human and model critique is the metric you optimise; meta-prompting can rewrite the judge prompt to raise it.
Reference-based metrics compare to a known correct answer; reference-free metrics score qualities like tone or safety where many answers are valid.
The four common mistakes are tool-first thinking, generic-metrics obsession, avoiding your data, and unaligned judges.

sections.title: The questions evaluations exist to answer
sections.summary: Every engineer building on LLMs eventually hits a wall of questions that logs alone cannot answer.

sections.title: The three core challenges of LLM development
sections.summary: Understanding your data, closing the specification gap, and coping with inconsistent behaviour — these are what evaluation exists to address.

sections.title: What an eval is, and the analyze-measure-improve cycle
sections.summary: An eval is a systematic measurement of one specific quality aspect; the working loop is collect failures, turn them into metrics, then improve.

sections.title: Level 1: unit tests as evals
sections.summary: Fast, cheap Python assertions over structured output, run on every code and prompt change.

sections.title: Level 2: humans first, then an aligned model judge

sections.title: Four mistakes, and the principles that avoid them
